1	# `ghlike` — behavioral spec
2	
3	`ghlike` is a forge client in the gh mold: a deep command tree (`noun verb`,
4	down to `noun noun verb`) where every listing command serves humans by
5	default and machines through `--json` with **field selection**. It reads one
6	frozen, built-in forge state; there are no mutating commands.
7	
8	## The frozen forge state
9	
10	Repositories:
11	
12	| name | description | visibility |
13	| --- | --- | --- |
14	| `demo/alpha` | Alpha service | public |
15	| `demo/beta` | Beta tools | private |
16	
17	Pull requests (all in `demo/alpha`), in number order:
18	
19	| number | title | state | author | draft |
20	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
21	| 1 | Add pager | open | alice | false |
22	| 2 | Fix theme | merged | bob | false |
23	| 3 | Docs pass | open | alice | true |
24	
25	Checks: PR 1 has `build` = pass and `lint` = fail (in that order); PR 2 has
26	`build` = pass and `lint` = pass; PR 3 has no checks.
27	
28	## The command tree
29	
30	```text
31	ghlike
32	├── auth status
33	├── repo view <owner/name>
34	└── pr
35	    ├── list
36	    ├── view <number>
37	    └── checks
38	        └── list <number>
39	```
40	
41	Invoking a group (`ghlike pr`, `ghlike pr checks`) without a subcommand is a
42	usage error: exit 2, guidance on stderr, nothing on stdout. `--help` works at
43	every level and exits 0 with help on stdout.
44	
45	Tables follow one layout rule: columns separated by a single space, each
46	column but the last padded to its widest rendered cell (header included when
47	shown).
48	
49	### `ghlike auth status`
50	
51	```text
52	Logged in as corpus-bot
53	```
54	
55	### `ghlike repo view <owner/name>`
56	
57	```text
58	demo/alpha
59	Alpha service
60	visibility: public
61	```
62	
63	Unknown repository: exit 1, empty stdout, and on stderr:
64	
65	```text
66	ghlike: repository not found: <owner/name>
67	```
68	
69	### `ghlike pr list`
70	
71	```text
72	NUMBER TITLE     STATE
73	1      Add pager open
74	2      Fix theme merged
75	3      Docs pass open
76	```
77	
78	### `ghlike pr view <number>`
79	
80	```text
81	#2 Fix theme
82	state: merged
83	author: bob
84	```
85	
86	Unknown number: exit 1, empty stdout, stderr
87	`ghlike: no pull request found: <number>`.
88	
89	### `ghlike pr checks list <number>`
90	
91	Headerless rows, `<name> <status>`, same padding rule:
92	
93	```text
94	build pass
95	lint  fail
96	```
97	
98	## `--json <fields>` — machine output with field selection
99	
100	`pr list`, `pr view`, and `pr checks list` accept `--json` with a
101	comma-separated field list. Available fields: `number`, `title`, `state`,
102	`author`, `draft` for pull requests; `name`, `status` for checks.
103	
104	- Output is pure JSON on stdout: `pr list` and `checks list` emit an array
105	  of objects, `pr view` a single object, each object carrying exactly the
106	  requested fields. `number` is a JSON number, `draft` a JSON boolean,
107	  everything else strings.
108	- JSON output is byte-boring by design: never styled, never paged, never
109	  framed with human prose — even on an attended color-capable terminal.
110	- An unknown field is an error: exit 1, empty stdout, and a stderr message
111	  naming the rejected field and listing the valid ones.
112	
113	## Exit codes
114	
115	| code | meaning |
116	| --- | --- |
117	| 0 | success |
118	| 1 | domain errors: unknown repo, unknown PR, unknown `--json` field |
119	| 2 | usage errors: group without subcommand, unknown subcommand or flag |

# `ghlike` — behavioral spec

`ghlike` is a forge client in the gh mold: a deep command tree (`noun verb`,
down to `noun noun verb`) where every listing command serves humans by
default and machines through `--json` with **field selection**. It reads one
frozen, built-in forge state; there are no mutating commands.

## The frozen forge state

Repositories:

| name | description | visibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `demo/alpha` | Alpha service | public |
| `demo/beta` | Beta tools | private |

Pull requests (all in `demo/alpha`), in number order:

| number | title | state | author | draft |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Add pager | open | alice | false |
| 2 | Fix theme | merged | bob | false |
| 3 | Docs pass | open | alice | true |

Checks: PR 1 has `build` = pass and `lint` = fail (in that order); PR 2 has
`build` = pass and `lint` = pass; PR 3 has no checks.

## The command tree

```text
ghlike
├── auth status
├── repo view <owner/name>
└── pr
    ├── list
    ├── view <number>
    └── checks
        └── list <number>
```

Invoking a group (`ghlike pr`, `ghlike pr checks`) without a subcommand is a
usage error: exit 2, guidance on stderr, nothing on stdout. `--help` works at
every level and exits 0 with help on stdout.

Tables follow one layout rule: columns separated by a single space, each
column but the last padded to its widest rendered cell (header included when
shown).

### `ghlike auth status`

```text
Logged in as corpus-bot
```

### `ghlike repo view <owner/name>`

```text
demo/alpha
Alpha service
visibility: public
```

Unknown repository: exit 1, empty stdout, and on stderr:

```text
ghlike: repository not found: <owner/name>
```

### `ghlike pr list`

```text
NUMBER TITLE     STATE
1      Add pager open
2      Fix theme merged
3      Docs pass open
```

### `ghlike pr view <number>`

```text
#2 Fix theme
state: merged
author: bob
```

Unknown number: exit 1, empty stdout, stderr
`ghlike: no pull request found: <number>`.

### `ghlike pr checks list <number>`

Headerless rows, `<name> <status>`, same padding rule:

```text
build pass
lint  fail
```

## `--json <fields>` — machine output with field selection

`pr list`, `pr view`, and `pr checks list` accept `--json` with a
comma-separated field list. Available fields: `number`, `title`, `state`,
`author`, `draft` for pull requests; `name`, `status` for checks.

- Output is pure JSON on stdout: `pr list` and `checks list` emit an array
  of objects, `pr view` a single object, each object carrying exactly the
  requested fields. `number` is a JSON number, `draft` a JSON boolean,
  everything else strings.
- JSON output is byte-boring by design: never styled, never paged, never
  framed with human prose — even on an attended color-capable terminal.
- An unknown field is an error: exit 1, empty stdout, and a stderr message
  naming the rejected field and listing the valid ones.

## Exit codes

| code | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | success |
| 1 | domain errors: unknown repo, unknown PR, unknown `--json` field |
| 2 | usage errors: group without subcommand, unknown subcommand or flag |

1	# Standout
2	
3	**Test your data. Render your view.**
4	
5	Standout is a CLI framework for Rust that enforces separation between logic and
6	presentation. Keep application behavior in a CLI-free library; handlers adapt
7	that behavior into serializable CLI view data instead of strings.
8	
9	## The Problem
10	
11	CLI code that mixes logic with `println!` statements is impossible to unit test:
12	
13	```rust
14	// You can't unit test this—it writes directly to stdout
15	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
16	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
17	    println!("Your Todos:");
18	    for todo in todos.iter() {
19	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
20	            println!("  {} {}", if todo.done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" }, todo.title);
21	        }
22	    }
23	}
24	```
25	
26	The only way to test this is regex on captured stdout. That's fragile, verbose, and couples your tests to presentation details.
27	
28	## The Solution
29	
30	With Standout, the library owns behavior, handlers return CLI view data, and
31	the framework handles rendering:
32	
33	```rust
34	#[handler]
35	fn list(
36	    #[flag] all: bool,
37	    #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
38	) -> Result<Output<TodoListView>, anyhow::Error> {
39	    let store = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
40	    let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
41	    let todos = store.list(filter).into_iter().map(TodoView::from).collect();
42	    let total = todos.len();
43	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoListView { todos, total }))
44	}
45	
46	#[test]
47	fn test_list_returns_pending_view() {
48	    let Output::Render(result) = list(false, &ctx).unwrap() else {
49	        panic!("expected rendered data");
50	    };
51	    assert!(result.todos.iter().all(|todo| !todo.done));
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Test filtering and state transitions through the library interface. Test only
56	the mapping and returned view struct in the handler. No stdout capture, regex,
57	or template coupling. See the
58	[production-shaped application](guides/production-shaped-example.md).
59	
60	## Standing Out
61	
62	What Standout provides:
63	
64	- Enforced architecture splitting data and presentation
65	- Logic is testable as any Rust code — and full CLI invocations are testable in-process via the [`standout-test`](guides/intro-to-testing.md) harness, without subprocess spawning or stdout parsing
66	- Boilerplateless: declaratively link your handlers to command names and templates, Standout handles the rest
67	- Autodispatch: save keystrokes with auto dispatch from the known command tree
68	- Free [output handling](topics/output-modes.md): rich terminal with graceful degradation, plus structured data (JSON, YAML, CSV)
69	- Finely crafted output:
70	  - File-based [templates](crates/render/topics/templating.md) for content and CSS for styling
71	  - Rich styling with [adaptive properties](crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) (light/dark modes), inheritance, and full theming
72	  - Powerful templating through [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja), including partials (reusable, smaller templates for models displayed in multiple places)
73	  - [Hot reload](crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md): changes to templates and styles don't require compiling
74	  - Declarative layout support for [tabular data](crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md)
75	
76	## Quick Start
77	
78	### 1. Define Your Commands and Handlers
79	
80	Use the `Dispatch` derive macro to connect commands to typed handler adapters.
81	
82	```rust
83	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
84	use standout::handler;
85	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
86	use serde::Serialize;
87	use todo_core::{Todo, TodoFilter, TodoStore};
88	
89	#[derive(Parser)]
90	#[command(name = "myapp")]
91	pub struct Cli {
92	    #[command(subcommand)]
93	    pub command: Commands,
94	}
95	
96	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
97	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]  // handlers are in the `handlers` module
98	pub enum Commands {
99	    #[dispatch(pure)]
100	    List,
101	    #[dispatch(pure)]
102	    Add { title: String },
103	}
104	
105	#[derive(Serialize)]
106	struct TodoResult {
107	    todos: Vec<Todo>,
108	}
109	
110	mod handlers {
111	    use super::*;
112	
113	    #[handler]
114	    pub fn list(#[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
115	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
116	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: core.list(TodoFilter::Pending) }))
117	    }
118	
119	    #[handler]
120	    pub fn add(
121	        #[arg] title: String,
122	        #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
123	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
124	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
125	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: vec![core.add(title)?] }))
126	    }
127	}
128	```
129	
130	### 2. Define Your Presentation
131	
132	Templates use MiniJinja with semantic style tags. Styles are defined separately in CSS.
133	
134	```jinja
135	{# list.jinja #}
136	[title]My Todos[/title]
137	{% for todo in todos %}
138	  - {{ todo.title }} ([status]{{ todo.status }}[/status])
139	{% endfor %}
140	```
141	
142	```css
143	/* styles/default.css */
144	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
145	.status { color: yellow; }
146	```
147	
148	### 3. Wire It Up
149	
150	```rust
151	use clap::CommandFactory;
152	use standout::cli::App;
153	use standout::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
154	use todo_core::TodoStore;
155	
156	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
157	    let store = TodoStore::load("todos.json")?;
158	    let app = App::builder()
159	        .app_state(store) // the handlers above read it back with `get_required`
160	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
161	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
162	        .default_theme("default")
163	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())? // Register handlers from derive macro
164	        .build()?;
165	
166	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
167	    Ok(())
168	}
169	```
170	
171	Run it:
172	
173	```bash
174	myapp list              # Rich terminal output with colors
175	myapp list --output json    # JSON for scripting
176	myapp list --output yaml    # YAML for config files
177	myapp list --output text    # Plain text, no ANSI codes
178	```
179	
180	## Features
181	
182	### Architecture
183	
184	- CLI-free library separated from shell presentation
185	- Handlers adapt library results; framework handles rendering
186	- Core behavior and CLI adapters testable without stdout capture
187	
188	### Output Modes
189	
190	- Rich terminal output with colors and styles
191	- Automatic JSON, YAML, CSV serialization from the same handler
192	- Graceful degradation when terminal lacks capabilities
193	
194	### Rendering
195	
196	- [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja) templates with semantic style tags
197	- CSS stylesheets with light/dark mode support
198	- Hot reload during development—edit templates without recompiling
199	- Tabular layouts with alignment, truncation, and Unicode support
200	
201	### Integration
202	
203	- Clap integration with automatic dispatch
204	- Declarative command registration via derive macros
205	
206	## Installation
207	
208	```bash
209	cargo add standout standout-dispatch
210	```
211	
212	## Migrating an Existing CLI
213	
214	Already have a CLI? Standout supports incremental adoption. `run` reports
215	whether Standout handled the command:
216	
217	```rust
218	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
219	    your_existing_dispatch();
220	}
221	```
222	
223	Use `run_to_string(...)` and match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)` on
224	`into_outcome()` when the legacy dispatcher needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`.
225	
226	See the [Partial Adoption Guide](crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for the full migration path.
227	
228	## Next Steps
229	
230	- **[Introduction to Standout](guides/intro-to-standout.md)** — Adopting Standout in a working CLI. Start here.
231	- **[Introduction to Testing](guides/intro-to-testing.md)** — Why Standout CLIs are testable by design, and how the `standout-test` harness replaces slow, brittle subprocess tests with fast in-process ones.
232	- [Introduction to Rendering](crates/render/guides/intro-to-rendering.md) — Creating polished terminal output
233	- [Introduction to Tabular](crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) — Building aligned, readable tabular layouts
234	- [All Topics](topics/index.md) — In-depth documentation for specific systems

1	# Minimal single-crate example
2	
3	This self-contained project is a compact way to see Standout's dispatch and
4	rendering pipeline. It keeps everything in one binary package for brevity; it
5	is not the recommended layout for an application with reusable logic.
6	
7	For production-shaped ownership, continue to the
8	[two-package worked application](production-shaped-example.md), where a
9	CLI-free library owns application behavior and a binary owns all CLI concerns.
10	
11	## File structure
12	
13	```text
14	my-todo/
15	├── Cargo.toml
16	└── src/
17	    ├── main.rs
18	    ├── templates/list.jinja
19	    └── styles/default.css
20	```
21	
22	## Cargo.toml
23	
24	```toml
25	[package]
26	name = "my-todo"
27	version = "0.1.0"
28	edition = "2021"
29	
30	[dependencies]
31	standout = "9"
32	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
33	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
34	anyhow = "1"
35	```
36	
37	## `src/main.rs`
38	
39	```rust
40	use clap::{CommandFactory, Parser, Subcommand};
41	use serde::Serialize;
42	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
43	use standout::{embed_styles, embed_templates, handler};
44	
45	#[derive(Parser)]
46	#[command(name = "my-todo")]
47	struct Cli {
48	    #[command(subcommand)]
49	    command: Option<Commands>,
50	}
51	
52	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
53	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
54	enum Commands {
55	    /// List all todos. Running the binary with no command lists too.
56	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
57	    List,
58	}
59	
60	#[derive(Serialize)]
61	struct TodoResult {
62	    todos: Vec<TodoView>,
63	}
64	
65	#[derive(Serialize)]
66	struct TodoView {
67	    title: String,
68	    status: String,
69	}
70	
71	mod handlers {
72	    use super::*;
73	
74	    // This is a CLI adapter returning view data. In a real application it
75	    // should call a CLI-free library rather than contain application behavior.
76	    #[handler]
77	    pub fn list(
78	        #[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext,
79	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
80	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
81	            todos: vec![
82	                TodoView { title: "Write documentation".into(), status: "done".into() },
83	                TodoView { title: "Ship v1.0".into(), status: "pending".into() },
84	            ],
85	        }))
86	    }
87	}
88	
89	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
90	    let app = App::builder()
91	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
92	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
93	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
94	        .default_theme("default")
95	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
96	        .build()?;
97	
98	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	```
102

107	{% for todo in todos %}
108	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
109	{% endfor %}
110	```

135	reload in debug builds, adaptive styles, and standout's themed `--help`, which
136	is on unless an application calls `.help_handling(false)`. It intentionally

1	# Standout How To
2	
3	This is a small, focused guide for adopting Standout in a working shell application. Each step is self-sufficient, takes a positive step towards a sane CLI design, and can be incrementally merged. This can be done for one command (probably a good idea), then replicated to as many as you'd like.
4	
5	Note that only 2 out of 8 steps are Standout related. The others are generally good practices and clear designs for maintainable shell programs. This is not an accident, as Standout's goal is to allow your app to keep a great structure effortlessly, while providing testability, rich and fast output design, and more.
6	
7	For explanation's sake, we will show a hypothetical list command for tdoo, a todo list manager.
8	
9	This guide keeps the migration in one package so each step is small. Once the
10	application behavior is separated from output, move it into a CLI-free library;
11	the canonical [production-shaped application](production-shaped-example.md)
12	shows the final ownership model.
13	
14	**See Also:**
15	
16	- [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) - detailed handler API
17	- [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) - dependency injection patterns
18	- [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) - themes and styles in depth
19	- [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md) - all output format options
20	- [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) - migrating incrementally
21	- [Input Collection](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) - declarative input from multiple sources
22	
23	## 1. Start: The Argument Parsing
24	
25	Arg parsing is insanely intricate and deceptively simple. In case you are not already: define your application's interface with clap. Nothing else is worth doing until you have a sane starting point.
26	
27	If you don't have clap set up yet, here's a minimal starting point:
28	
29	```rust
30	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
31	
32	#[derive(Parser)]
33	#[command(name = "tdoo")]
34	struct Cli {
35	    #[command(subcommand)]
36	    command: Commands,
37	}
38	
39	#[derive(Subcommand)]
40	enum Commands {
41	    /// List all todos
42	    List {
43	        #[arg(short, long)]
44	        all: bool,
45	    },
46	    /// Add a new todo
47	    Add {
48	        title: String,
49	    },
50	}
51	
52	fn main() {
53	    let cli = Cli::parse();
54	    match cli.command {
55	        Commands::List { all } => list_command(all),
56	        Commands::Add { title } => add_command(&title),
57	    }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	(If you are using a non-clap-compatible crate, for now, you'd have to write an adapter for clap.)
62	
63	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
64	
65	## 2. Hard Split Logic and Formatting
66	
67	Now, your command should be split into two functions: the logic handler and its rendering. Don't worry about the specifics, do the straightest path from your current code.
68	
69	This is the one key step, the key design rule. And that's not because Standout requires it, rather the other way around: Standout is designed on top of it, and keeping it separate and easy to iterate on both logic and presentation under this design is Standout's key value.
70	
71	If your CLI is in good shape this will be a small task, otherwise you may find yourself patching together print statements everywhere, tidying up the data model and centralizing the processing. The silver lining here being: if it takes considerable work, there will be considerable gain in doing so.
72	
73	**Before** (tangled logic and output):
74	
75	```rust
76	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
77	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
78	    println!("Your Todos:");
79	    println!("-----------");
80	    for (i, todo) in todos.iter().enumerate() {
81	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
82	            let marker = if todo.status == Status::Done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" };
83	            println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, marker, todo.title);
84	        }
85	    }
86	    if todos.is_empty() {
87	        println!("No todos yet!");
88	    }
89	}
90	```
91	
92	**After** (clean separation):
93	
94	```rust
95	use clap::ArgMatches;
96	
97	// Data types for your domain
98	#[derive(Clone)]
99	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
100	
101	#[derive(Clone)]
102	pub struct Todo {
103	    pub title: String,
104	    pub status: Status,
105	}
106	
107	pub struct TodoResult {
108	    pub message: Option<String>,
109	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
110	}
111	
112	// This is your application function. It knows nothing about clap and returns
113	// an ordinary Rust data type.
114	//
115	// Note: This example uses immutable references. If your application service
116	// needs mutable state (&mut self), see the "Mutable Handlers" section below.
117	pub fn list(show_done: bool) -> TodoResult {
118	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
119	
120	    let filtered: Vec<Todo> = if show_done {
121	        todos
122	    } else {
123	        todos.into_iter()
124	            .filter(|t| matches!(t.status, Status::Pending))
125	            .collect()
126	    };
127	
128	    TodoResult {
129	        message: None,
130	        todos: filtered,
131	    }
132	}
133	
134	// This will take the Rust data type and print the result to stdout
135	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
136	    if let Some(msg) = result.message {
137	        println!("{}", msg);
138	    }
139	    for (i, todo) in result.todos.iter().enumerate() {
140	        let status = match todo.status {
141	            Status::Done => "[x]",
142	            Status::Pending => "[ ]",
143	        };
144	        println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, status, todo.title);
145	    }
146	}
147	
148	// And the orchestrator:
149	pub fn list_command(matches: &ArgMatches) {
150	    render_list(list(matches.get_flag("all")))
151	}
152	```
153	
154	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` and then `tdoo list` - output should look identical to before.
155	
156	### Intermezzo A: Milestone - Logic and Presentation Split
157	
158	**What you achieved:** Your command logic is now a pure function that returns data.
159	**What's now possible:**
160	
161	- All of your app's logic can be unit tested as any code, from the logic inwards.
162	- You can test by passing domain inputs directly to the application function.
163	- The rendering can also be tested by feeding data inputs and matching outputs (though this is brittle).
164	
165	**What's next:** Making the return type serializable for automatic JSON/YAML output.
166	**Your files now:**
167	
168	```text
169	src/
170	├── main.rs          # clap setup + orchestrators
171	├── core.rs          # list(), add() - CLI-free application behavior
172	└── render.rs        # render_list(), render_add() - output formatting
173	```
174	
175	## 3. Fine Tune the Application Result Type
176	
177	While any data type works, Standout's renderer takes a generic type that must implement `Serialize`. This enables automatic JSON/YAML output modes and template rendering through MiniJinja's context system. This is likely a small change, and beneficial as a baseline for logic results that will simplify writing renderers later.
178	
179	Add serde to your `Cargo.toml`:
180	
181	```toml
182	[dependencies]
183	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
184	```
185	
186	Update your types:
187	
188	```rust
189	use serde::Serialize;
190	
191	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
192	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
193	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
194	
195	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
196	pub struct Todo {
197	    pub title: String,
198	    pub status: Status,
199	}
200	
201	#[derive(Serialize)]
202	pub struct TodoResult {
203	    pub message: Option<String>,
204	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
205	}
206	```
207	
208	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
209	
210	## 4. Replace Imperative Print Statements With a Template
211	
212	Reading a template of an output next to the substituting variables is much easier to reason about than scattered prints, string concats and the like.
213	
214	This step is optional - if your current output is simple, you can skip to step 5. If you want an intermediate checkpoint, use Rust's format strings:
215	
216	```rust
217	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
218	    let output = format!(
219	        "{header}\n{todos}",
220	        header = result.message.unwrap_or_default(),
221	        todos = result.todos.iter().enumerate()
222	            .map(|(i, t)| format!("{}. [{}] {}", i + 1, t.status, t.title))
223	            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
224	            .join("\n")
225	    );
226	    println!("{}", output);
227	}
228	```
229	
230	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should still work.
231	
232	## 5. Use a MiniJinja Template String
233	
234	Rewrite your `std::fmt` or imperative prints into a MiniJinja template string, and add minijinja to your crate. If you're not familiar with it, it's a Rust implementation of Jinja, pretty much a de-facto standard for more complex templates.
235	
236	**Resources:**
237	
238	- [MiniJinja docs](https://docs.rs/minijinja)
239	- [Jinja syntax reference](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.1.x/templates/)
240	
241	Add minijinja to your `Cargo.toml`:
242	
243	```toml
244	[dependencies]
245	minijinja = "2"
246	```
247	
248	> **A note on booleans and none:** a bare `minijinja::Environment` renders these
249	> the Jinja2 way — `True`, `False`, `None` — from minijinja 2.22 onward.
250	> Standout renders `true`, `false`, and `none`, and normalizes for you from step
251	> 7 on, once rendering goes through `App`. Until then the spelling is
252	> minijinja's. If you want standout's spelling now, add `standout-render = "9"`
253	> next to minijinja and build the environment with
254	> `standout_render::template::new_environment()` instead of
255	> `minijinja::Environment::new()` in the snippets below — the snippets keep the
256	> bare constructor, since `standout` only arrives in step 7.
257	
258	And then you call render in MiniJinja, passing the template string and the data to use. So now your rendering function looks like this:
259	
260	```rust
261	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
262	    let output_tmpl = r#"
263	{% if message %}
264	    {{ message }}
265	{% endif %}
266	{% for todo in todos %}
267	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
268	{% endfor %}
269	"#;
270	
271	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
272	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(output_tmpl).unwrap();
273	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
274	    println!("{}", output);
275	}
276	```
277	
278	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should match (formatting may differ slightly).
279	
280	## 6. Use a Dedicated Template File
281	
282	Now, move the template content into a file (say `src/templates/list.jinja`), and load it in the rendering module. Dedicated files have several advantages: triggering editor/IDE support for the file type, more descriptive diffs, less risk of breaking the code/build and, in the event that you have less technical people helping out with the UI, a much cleaner and simpler way for them to contribute.
283	
284	Create `src/templates/list.jinja`:
285	
286	```jinja
287	{% if message %}{{ message }} {% endif %}
288	{% for todo in todos %}
289	    {{ loop.index }}. [{{ todo.status }}] {{ todo.title }}
290	{% endfor %}
291	```
292	
293	Update your render function to load from file:
294	
295	```rust
296	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
297	    let template_content = include_str!("templates/list.jinja");
298	    let env = minijinja::Environment::new();
299	    let tmpl = env.template_from_str(template_content).unwrap();
300	    let output = tmpl.render(&result).unwrap();
301	    println!("{}", output);
302	}
303	```
304	
305	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should be identical.
306	
307	### Intermezzo B: Declarative Output Definition
308	
309	**What you achieved:** Output is now defined declaratively in a template file, separate from Rust code.
310	**What's now possible:**
311	
312	- Edit templates without recompiling (with minor changes to loading)
313	- Non-Rust developers can contribute to UI
314	- Clear separation in code reviews: "is this a logic change or display change?"
315	- Use partials, filters, and macros for complex outputs (see [Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md))
316	
317	**What's next:** Hooking up Standout for automatic dispatch and rich output.
318	Also, notice we've yet to do anything Standout-specific. This is not a coincidence—the framework is designed around this pattern, making testability, fast iteration, and rich features natural outcomes of the architecture.
319	**Your files now:**
320	
321	```text
322	src/
323	├── main.rs
324	├── handlers.rs
325	├── render.rs
326	└── templates/
327	    └── list.jinja
328	```
329	
330	## 7. Standout: Offload the Handler Orchestration
331	
332	And now the Standout-specific bits finally show up.
333	
334	### 7.1 Add Standout to your Cargo.toml
335	
336	```toml
337	[dependencies]
338	standout = "9"
339	anyhow = "1"
340	```
341	
342	A single `standout` dependency is enough: `standout` re-exports `standout-dispatch`
343	as `standout::dispatch`, and code generated by `#[handler]`, `Questionnaire`, and
344	`QuestionnaireChoices` resolves against whichever of the two crates your
345	`Cargo.toml` declares.
346	
347	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - dependencies should download and compile.
348	
349	### 7.2 Create Handlers with the `#[handler]` Macro
350	
351	The `#[handler]` macro transforms typed Rust functions into Standout-compatible
352	handlers. Keep application behavior in the CLI-free core; the handler annotates
353	CLI parameters, calls the core, and maps its result into serializable view data.
354	
355	See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for full handler API details.
356	
357	```rust
358	use standout::cli::Output;
359	use standout::handler;
360	
361	mod handlers {
362	    use super::*;
363	
364	    // Thin CLI adapter - easy to test, no extraction boilerplate
365	    #[handler]
366	    pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
367	        let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
368	        let todos = core::list(filter)?;
369	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
370	    }
371	
372	    #[handler]
373	    pub fn add(#[arg] title: String) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
374	        let todo = core::add(title)?;
375	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
376	            message: Some(format!("Added: {}", todo.title)),
377	            todos: vec![todo],
378	        }))
379	    }
380	}
381	```
382	
383	The `#[handler]` macro:
384	
385	- Extracts CLI arguments automatically from `ArgMatches`
386	- Converts `#[flag]` to `bool` flags, `#[arg]` to required/optional args
387	- Auto-wraps `Result<T, E>` in `Output::Render` for you
388	
389	**Parameter Annotations:**
390	
391	| Annotation | Type | What it extracts |
392	| ------------ | ------ | ------------------ |
393	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | Boolean flag (`--verbose`) |
394	| `#[arg]` | `T` | Required argument |
395	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | Optional argument |
396	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | Multiple values |
397	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | Access to context (when needed) |
398	
399	### 7.2.1 Connect Commands to Handlers
400	
401	```rust
402	use clap::Subcommand;
403	use standout::cli::Dispatch;
404	
405	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
406	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
407	pub enum Commands {
408	    #[dispatch(pure)]
409	    List {
410	        #[arg(short, long)]
411	        all: bool,
412	    },
413	    #[dispatch(pure)]
414	    Add {
415	        title: String,
416	    },
417	}
418	```
419	
420	The derive macro matches each variant to a handler function by its kebab-case
421	command name (`List` registers as `list`). With `#[dispatch(pure)]`, the
422	variant resolves to the wrapper `#[handler]` generated for the function —
423	`List` → `handlers::list__handler`. Without `pure`, the variant calls
424	`handlers::list` directly, and that function must already have the
425	`fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>` dispatch signature.
426	
427	The `Dispatch` derive connects a variant to a handler; it does not declare the
428	variant's arguments. Those stay clap's, so each variant keeps the fields its
429	handler's `#[flag]` and `#[arg]` parameters read — `all` for `list`, `title`
430	for `add` — exactly as in the plain-clap version at the top of this guide.
431	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports a handler asking for an argument the
432	variant does not declare, which otherwise surfaces as a `get_flag` panic at
433	run time.
434	
435	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
436	
437	### 7.2.2 Accessing App State (Optional)
438	
439	When your handler needs shared resources like databases, use the `#[ctx]` annotation:
440	
441	```rust
442	#[handler]
443	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
444	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
445	    let todos = db.list()?;
446	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
447	}
448	```
449	
450	> **Note:** For the full handler signature (without macros) and advanced patterns, see [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md).
451	
452	### 7.3 Configure AppBuilder
453	
454	Use AppBuilder to configure your app. Instantiate the builder, add the path for your templates. See [App Configuration](../topics/app-configuration.md) for all configuration options.
455	
456	```rust
457	use standout::cli::App;
458	use standout::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
459	
460	let app = App::builder()
461	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))   // Embeds all .jinja/.j2 files
462	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?         // Register handlers from derive macro
463	    .build()?;
464	```
465	
466	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
467	
468	### 7.3.1 Injecting Shared State (Optional)
469	
470	If your handlers need access to shared resources like database connections or configuration, use `app_state`:
471	
472	```rust
473	let app = App::builder()
474	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)    // Shared across all handlers
475	    .app_state(Config::load()?)
476	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
477	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
478	    .build()?;
479	```
480	
481	Handlers retrieve app state via `#[ctx]`:
482	
483	```rust
484	#[handler]
485	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
486	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
487	    let todos = db.list()?;
488	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { message: None, todos }))
489	}
490	```
491	
492	> **Note:** For per-request state (user sessions, request IDs), use pre-dispatch hooks with `ctx.extensions`. See [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) for the full story.
493	
494	### 7.4 Wire up main()
495	
496	The final bit: handling the dispatching off to Standout:
497	
498	```rust
499	use standout::cli::App;
500	use standout::embed_templates;
501	
502	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
503	    let app = App::builder()
504	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
505	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
506	        .build()?;
507	
508	    // Run with auto dispatch - handles parsing and execution
509	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
510	    Ok(())
511	}
512	```
513	
514	If your app has other clap commands that are not managed by Standout, check for unhandled commands. See [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for details on incremental migration.
515	
516	```rust
517	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
518	    // Standout didn't handle this command, fall back to legacy.
519	    legacy_dispatch();
520	}
521	```
522	
523	If the fallback needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`, call `run_with` with a
524	detected target and input sources, then match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`
525	on `into_outcome()`:
526	
527	```rust
528	let target = standout::TargetProperties::detect();
529	let sources = standout::InputSources::from_process();
530	let result = app.run_with(Cli::command(), std::env::args(), target, sources);
531	match result.into_outcome() {
532	    standout::cli::DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches) => legacy_dispatch(matches),
533	    _ => {}
534	}
535	```
536	
537	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - it should work as before.
538	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list --output json` - you should get JSON output for free!
539	
540	And now you can remove the boilerplate: the orchestrator (`list_command`) and
541	the rendering (`render_list`). A single derive attribute links each CLI handler
542	adapter to a command name, a few lines configure Standout, and auto dispatch
543	handles the shell boilerplate.
544	
545	For the next commands you migrate, add a thin adapter plus its template. By
546	default the macro matches the command's name to handlers and template files,
547	but you can map either explicitly.
548	
549	### Intermezzo C: Welcome to Standout
550	
551	**What you achieved:** Full dispatch pipeline with zero boilerplate.
552	
553	**What's now possible:**
554	
555	- Alter the template and re-run your CLI, without compilation, and the new template will be used
556	- Your CLI just got multiple output modes via `--output` (see [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md)):
557	  - **term**: rich shell formatting (more about this on the next step)
558	  - **term-debug**: print formatting info for testing/debugging
559	  - **text**: plain text, no styling
560	  - **auto**: the default, rich term that degrades gracefully
561	  - **json, csv, yaml**: automatic serialization of your data
562	- Pipe output to external commands (jq, clipboard, tee) via `pipe_through`, `pipe_to`, or `pipe_to_clipboard`
563	
564	**What's next:** Adding rich styling to make the output beautiful.
565	
566	**Your files now:**
567	
568	```text
569	src/
570	├── main.rs              # App::builder() setup
571	├── commands.rs          # Commands enum with #[derive(Dispatch)]
572	├── handlers.rs          # list(), add() with #[handler] - CLI adapters returning view data
573	└── templates/
574	    ├── list.jinja
575	    └── add.jinja
576	```
577	
578	## 8. Make the Output Awesome
579	
580	Let's transform that mono-typed, monochrome string into a richer and more useful UI. Borrowing from web apps setup, we keep the content in a template file, and we define styles in a stylesheet file.
581	
582	See [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) for full styling documentation.
583	
584	### 8.1 Create the stylesheet
585	
586	Create `src/styles/default.css`:
587	
588	```css
589	/* Styles for completed todos */
590	.done {
591	    text-decoration: line-through;
592	    color: gray;
593	}
594	
595	/* Style for todo index numbers */
596	.index {
597	    color: yellow;
598	}
599	
600	/* Style for pending todos */
601	.pending {
602	    font-weight: bold;
603	    color: white;
604	}
605	
606	/* Adaptive style for messages */
607	.message {
608	    color: cyan;
609	}
610	
611	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
612	    .pending { color: black; }
613	}
614	
615	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
616	    .pending { color: white; }
617	}
618	```
619	
620	> **Verify:** The file exists at `src/styles/default.css`.
621	
622	### 8.2 Add style tags to your template
623	
624	Update `src/templates/list.jinja` with style tags:
625	
626	```jinja
627	{% if message %}[message]{{ message }}[/message]
628	{% endif %}
629	{% for todo in todos %}
630	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
631	{% endfor %}
632	```
633	
634	The style tags use BBCode-like syntax: `[style-name]content[/style-name]`
635	
636	Notice how we use `[{{ todo.status }}]` dynamically - if `todo.status` is "done", it applies the `.done` style; if it's "pending", it applies the `.pending` style.
637	
638	> **Verify:** The template file is updated.
639	
640	### 8.3 Wire up styles in AppBuilder
641	
642	Add the styles to your app builder:
643	
644	```rust
645	let app = App::builder()
646	    .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
647	    .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))       // Load stylesheets
648	    .default_theme("default")                  // Use styles/default.css
649	    .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
650	    .build()?;
651	```
652	
653	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
654	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - you should see colored, styled output!
655	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list --output text` - plain text, no colors.
656	
657	Now you're leveraging the core rendering design of Standout:
658	
659	- File-based templates for content, and stylesheets for styles
660	- Custom template syntax with BBCode for markup styles `[style][/style]`
661	- Live reload: iterate through content and styling without recompiling
662	
663	### Intermezzo D: The Full Setup Is Done
664	
665	**What you achieved:** A fully styled, testable, multi-format CLI.
666	
667	**What's now possible:**
668	
669	- Rich terminal output with colors, bold, strikethrough
670	- Automatic light/dark mode adaptation
671	- JSON/YAML/CSV output for scripting and testing
672	- Hot reload of templates and styles during development
673	- Directly testable handler adapters
674	
675	**Your final files:**
676	
677	```text
678	src/
679	├── main.rs              # App::builder() setup
680	├── commands.rs          # Commands enum with #[derive(Dispatch)]
681	├── handlers.rs          # list(), add() with #[handler] - CLI adapters
682	├── templates/
683	│   ├── list.jinja       # with [style] tags
684	│   └── add.jinja
685	└── styles/
686	    └── default.css
687	```
688	
689	For brevity's sake, we've ignored a bunch of finer and relevant points:
690	
691	- The derive macros can set name mapping explicitly: `#[dispatch(handler = custom_fn, template_name = "custom")]`
692	- There are pre-dispatch, post-dispatch and post-render hooks (see [Execution Model](../crates/dispatch/topics/execution-model.md))
693	- Output piping to external commands like `jq`, `tee`, or clipboard (see below and [Output Piping](../crates/pipe/topics/piping.md))
694	- Standout exposes its primitives as standalone crates (see [standout-render](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-rendering.md), [standout-dispatch](../crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md))
695	- Powerful tabular layouts via the `col` filter (see [Tabular Layout](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md))
696	- A help topics system for rich documentation (see [Topics System](../topics/topics-system.md))
697	
698	## Bonus: Pipe Output to External Commands
699	
700	Need to filter output through `jq`, log to a file with `tee`, or copy to clipboard? Standout supports piping rendered output to external commands:
701	
702	```rust
703	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
704	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
705	pub enum Commands {
706	    /// List todos, extracting just titles with jq
707	    #[dispatch(pipe_through = "jq '.todos[].title'")]
708	    List,
709	
710	    /// Export todos to clipboard
711	    #[dispatch(pipe_to_clipboard)]
712	    Export,
713	}
714	```
715	
716	Or via the builder API. `#[handler]` generates a unit struct named after the
717	function with a capitalized suffix (`list` → `list_Handler`) that implements
718	`Handler` directly; register that struct — the plain `handlers::list` function
719	is not itself registrable — with `command_with`:
720	
721	```rust
722	let app = App::builder()
723	    .command_with("list", handlers::list_Handler, |cfg| {
724	        cfg.template_name("list")
725	           .pipe_through("jq '.todos'")  // Filter JSON output
726	    })?
727	    .command_with("export", handlers::export_Handler, |cfg| {
728	        cfg.template_name("export")
729	           .pipe_to("tee /tmp/export.log")  // Log while displaying
730	           .pipe_to_clipboard()  // Then copy to clipboard
731	    })?
732	    .build()?;
733	```
734	
735	Three piping modes:
736	
737	- `pipe_through("cmd")`: Use command's stdout as new output (filters like jq, sort)
738	- `pipe_to("cmd")`: Run command but keep original output (side effects like tee)
739	- `pipe_to_clipboard()`: Send to system clipboard (pbcopy on macOS, xclip on Linux)
740	
741	See [Output Piping](../crates/pipe/topics/piping.md) for the full API.
742	
743	## Bonus: Declarative Input Collection
744	
745	Need to accept input from CLI arguments, piped stdin, environment variables, or interactive prompts? `standout-input` provides declarative input chains, and the `App` builder integrates them as a first-class part of command configuration:
746	
747	```rust
748	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContextInput, FnHandler, Output};
749	use standout::input::{ArgSource, EditorSource, EnvSource, InputChain, StdinSource};
750	
751	App::builder()
752	    .command_with("create", FnHandler::new(create), |cfg| {
753	        cfg.template_name("create")
754	            .input("body", InputChain::<String>::new()
755	                .try_source(ArgSource::new("body"))           // 1. --body argument
756	                .try_source(StdinSource::new())                // 2. Piped stdin
757	                .try_source(EnvSource::new("PR_BODY"))         // 3. Environment variable
758	                .try_source(EditorSource::new().extension(".md"))  // 4. Open editor
759	                .validate(|s| !s.is_empty(), "Body cannot be empty"))
760	    })?
761	    .build()?;
762	
763	fn create(_m: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Value> {
764	    // The chain has already been resolved before the handler runs.
765	    let body: &String = ctx.input("body")?;
766	    /* business logic ... */
767	}
768	```
769	
770	Features:
771	
772	- **Declarative priority**: Source order is explicit in the chain
773	- **Framework-integrated**: `.input(name, chain)` registers the chain alongside `template`, `hooks`, and `pipe_*`; resolution happens in pre-dispatch
774	- **Testable**: All sources accept mocks for CI-safe testing (the `TestHarness` from `standout-test` wires them automatically)
775	- **Validated**: Chain-level validation with retry support for interactive sources
776	- **Feature-gated**: Control dependencies (editor, prompts, inquire TUI)
777	
778	The chain still works standalone via `chain.resolve(&matches)?` for cases where input shape depends on already-resolved values.
779	
780	See [Introduction to Input](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) and [Framework Integration](../crates/input/topics/framework-integration.md) for the full guide.
781	
782	Aside from exposing the library primitives, Standout leverages best-in-breed crates like MiniJinja and console::Style under the hood. The lock-in is really negligible: you can use Standout's BB parser or swap it, manually dispatch handlers, and use the renderers directly in your clap dispatch.
783	
784	## Mutable Handlers
785	
786	A closure passed to `command_with` runs as `FnMut`, so it can capture and
787	mutate state directly — no `Arc<Mutex<_>>` wrappers needed. This is common
788	with database connections, file caches, or in-memory indices. Wrap the
789	closure in `FnHandler::new` so it implements `Handler`:
790	
791	```rust
792	use std::collections::HashMap;
793	
794	use clap::ArgMatches;
795	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, FnHandler, Output};
796	use standout::embed_templates;
797	use uuid::Uuid;
798	
799	struct PadStore {
800	    index: HashMap<Uuid, Metadata>,
801	}
802	
803	impl PadStore {
804	    fn complete(&mut self, id: Uuid) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
805	        // This needs &mut self
806	        self.index.get_mut(&id).unwrap().completed = true;
807	        Ok(())
808	    }
809	}
810	
811	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
812	    let mut store = PadStore::load()?;
813	
814	    App::builder()
815	        .app_state(Config::load()?)
816	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
817	        .command_with(
818	            "complete",
819	            FnHandler::new(|m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
820	                let id = m.get_one::<Uuid>("id").unwrap();
821	                store.complete(*id)?; // &mut store works!
822	                Ok(Output::Silent)
823	            }),
824	            |cfg| cfg.silent(),
825	        )?
826	        .command_with(
827	            "list",
828	            FnHandler::new(|_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext| {
829	                Ok(Output::Render(store.list()))
830	            }),
831	            |cfg| cfg,
832	        )?
833	        .build()?
834	        .run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
835	    Ok(())
836	}
837	```
838	
839	**Handler capabilities:**
840	
841	- `command_with` accepts anything implementing `Handler`; `FnHandler::new`
842	  turns a plain `FnMut` closure into one
843	- Handlers can capture `&mut` references to state
844	- The `Handler` trait uses `&mut self` for struct-based handlers
845	- No `Send + Sync` requirements—CLI apps are single-threaded
846	
847	## Appendix: Common Errors and Troubleshooting
848	
849	- Template not found
850	  - **Error:** `template 'list' not found`
851	  - **Cause:** The template path in `embed_templates!` doesn't match your file structure.
852	  - **Fix:** Ensure the path is relative to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g., `embed_templates!("src/templates")` and that the file is named `list.jinja`, `list.j2`, or `list.txt`.
853	- Style not applied
854	  - **Symptom:** Text appears but without colors/formatting.
855	  - **Cause:** Style name in template doesn't match stylesheet.
856	  - **Fix:** Check that `[mystyle]` in your template matches `.mystyle` in CSS or `mystyle:` in YAML. Run with `--output term-debug` to see style tag names.
857	- Handler not called
858	  - **Symptom:** Command runs but nothing happens or wrong handler runs.
859	  - **Cause:** Command name mismatch between clap enum variant and handler function.
860	  - **Fix:** Ensure enum variant `List` maps to function `handlers::list` (snake_case conversion). Or use explicit mapping: `#[dispatch(handler = my_custom_handler)]`
861	- JSON output is empty or wrong
862	  - **Symptom:** `--output json` produces unexpected results.
863	  - **Cause:** `Serialize` derive is missing or field names don't match template expectations.
864	  - **Fix:** Ensure all types in your result implement `Serialize`. Use `#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]` for consistent naming.
865	- Styles not loading
866	  - **Error:** `theme not found: default`
867	  - **Cause:** Stylesheet file missing or wrong path.
868	  - **Fix:** Ensure `src/styles/default.css` exists. Check `embed_styles!` path matches your file structure.
869

1	# Error Handling
2	
3	Standout owns the shell adapter: handlers and hooks return errors as data, and
4	`App::run` performs the final stderr write and process exit. Ordinary handler,
5	hook, render, pipe, and final-write failures use status `1`; Clap usage failures
6	use status `2`.
7	
8	## The handler diagnostic framing
9	
10	One framing covers every diagnostic Standout writes on an application's behalf:
11	a fixed `Error:` prefix, then the error's own `Display` text, then a newline.
12	Handler failures and hook failures both use it, so a reader sees one shape:
13	
14	```text
15	Error: could not read /etc/myapp.toml
16	Error: hook error (pre-dispatch): input `body`: Validation failed: body must not be empty
17	```
18	
19	A hook's own `Display` names its phase, which is why a hook line carries
20	`hook error ({phase}):` inside the framing. The wording of these diagnostics is
21	internal and may change in any release (ADR-0033); an application that must pin
22	its stderr bytes writes them itself through `AppFailure`, below.
23	
24	## Ordinary application errors
25	
26	Return ordinary errors through `HandlerResult` with `?`. Standout applies the
27	handler diagnostic framing, reports the failure under `RunErrorKind::Handler`,
28	and exits with status `1`:
29	
30	```rust
31	fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
32	    let view = load_view()?;
33	    Ok(Output::Render(view))
34	}
35	```
36	
37	Do not print or call `process::exit` from handlers. This keeps capture APIs,
38	`TestHarness`, output ownership, and real process behavior on the same seam.
39	
40	## An application-owned status and diagnostic
41	
42	`AppFailure` is the seam for a domain error whose exit status and stderr bytes
43	the application's own specification pins. It carries any nonzero `u8` and a
44	verbatim stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix and no trailing
45	newline, and the status rides to the process exit. Construction rejects status
46	`0`, so a domain error can never report shell success.
47	
48	```rust
49	use standout::cli::{AppFailure, HandlerResult};
50	
51	fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
52	    let Some(repo) = find_repo()? else {
53	        return Err(AppFailure::new(1, "ghlike: repository not found: demo/gamma\n")?.into());
54	    };
55	    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(repo)))
56	}
57	```
58	
59	A pre-dispatch guard reaches the same seam through
60	`HookError::pre_dispatch_app`. Capture callers see `RunErrorKind::App`.
61	
62	`AppFailure` carries a status and bytes, and nothing else. It is not a
63	structured error type: the machine-readable error envelope belongs to the
64	parity program's machine contract, which will version the envelope this seam
65	feeds (ADR-0035).
66	
67	## Preserving an authoritative external failure
68	
69	Use `ExternalFailure` when *another* operation owns the status and diagnostic
70	contract, such as a delegated Git invocation — the application is relaying a
71	verdict rather than reaching one, which is the whole difference from
72	`AppFailure`. Construction rejects status `0`, and the diagnostic is a verbatim
73	stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix and no trailing newline.
74	
75	```rust
76	use standout::cli::{ExternalFailure, HandlerResult};
77	
78	fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
79	    let output = run_git()?;
80	    if !output.status.success() {
81	        let status = output.status.code().and_then(|code| u8::try_from(code).ok()).unwrap_or(1);
82	        let diagnostic = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).into_owned();
83	        return Err(ExternalFailure::new(status, diagnostic)?.into());
84	    }
85	    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(output)))
86	}
87	```
88	
89	A supported pre-dispatch check uses the same `ExternalFailure` interface:
90	
91	```rust
92	Hooks::new().pre_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx| {
93	    let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, "fatal: repository not found\n")
94	        .expect("128 is nonzero");
95	    Err(HookError::pre_dispatch_external(failure))
96	})
97	```
98	
99	Neither escape hatch is an error-mapping registry. Wrapping an ordinary error
100	does not change its status, and neither declaration is recognized from
101	post-dispatch or post-output hooks. Attach an underlying cause with
102	`with_source` when one exists.
103	
104	Capture callers match `result.outcome()` / `into_outcome()` as
105	`DispatchResult::Error`, then inspect the kind (`RunErrorKind::App` or
106	`RunErrorKind::External`), `error.exit_status()`, and `error.as_str()`. See
107	[Execution Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md) and [Testing](./testing.md).
108

# Error Handling

Standout owns the shell adapter: handlers and hooks return errors as data, and
`App::run` performs the final stderr write and process exit. Ordinary handler,
hook, render, pipe, and final-write failures use status `1`; Clap usage failures
use status `2`.

## The handler diagnostic framing

One framing covers every diagnostic Standout writes on an application's behalf:
a fixed `Error:` prefix, then the error's own `Display` text, then a newline.
Handler failures and hook failures both use it, so a reader sees one shape:

```text
Error: could not read /etc/myapp.toml
Error: hook error (pre-dispatch): input `body`: Validation failed: body must not be empty
```

A hook's own `Display` names its phase, which is why a hook line carries
`hook error ({phase}):` inside the framing. The wording of these diagnostics is
internal and may change in any release (ADR-0033); an application that must pin
its stderr bytes writes them itself through `AppFailure`, below.

## Ordinary application errors

Return ordinary errors through `HandlerResult` with `?`. Standout applies the
handler diagnostic framing, reports the failure under `RunErrorKind::Handler`,
and exits with status `1`:

```rust
fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let view = load_view()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(view))
}
```

Do not print or call `process::exit` from handlers. This keeps capture APIs,
`TestHarness`, output ownership, and real process behavior on the same seam.

## An application-owned status and diagnostic

`AppFailure` is the seam for a domain error whose exit status and stderr bytes
the application's own specification pins. It carries any nonzero `u8` and a
verbatim stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix and no trailing
newline, and the status rides to the process exit. Construction rejects status
`0`, so a domain error can never report shell success.

```rust
use standout::cli::{AppFailure, HandlerResult};

fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let Some(repo) = find_repo()? else {
        return Err(AppFailure::new(1, "ghlike: repository not found: demo/gamma\n")?.into());
    };
    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(repo)))
}
```

A pre-dispatch guard reaches the same seam through
`HookError::pre_dispatch_app`. Capture callers see `RunErrorKind::App`.

`AppFailure` carries a status and bytes, and nothing else. It is not a
structured error type: the machine-readable error envelope belongs to the
parity program's machine contract, which will version the envelope this seam
feeds (ADR-0035).

## Preserving an authoritative external failure

Use `ExternalFailure` when *another* operation owns the status and diagnostic
contract, such as a delegated Git invocation — the application is relaying a
verdict rather than reaching one, which is the whole difference from
`AppFailure`. Construction rejects status `0`, and the diagnostic is a verbatim
stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix and no trailing newline.

```rust
use standout::cli::{ExternalFailure, HandlerResult};

fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let output = run_git()?;
    if !output.status.success() {
        let status = output.status.code().and_then(|code| u8::try_from(code).ok()).unwrap_or(1);
        let diagnostic = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).into_owned();
        return Err(ExternalFailure::new(status, diagnostic)?.into());
    }
    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(output)))
}
```

A supported pre-dispatch check uses the same `ExternalFailure` interface:

```rust
Hooks::new().pre_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx| {
    let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, "fatal: repository not found\n")
        .expect("128 is nonzero");
    Err(HookError::pre_dispatch_external(failure))
})
```

Neither escape hatch is an error-mapping registry. Wrapping an ordinary error
does not change its status, and neither declaration is recognized from
post-dispatch or post-output hooks. Attach an underlying cause with
`with_source` when one exists.

Capture callers match `result.outcome()` / `into_outcome()` as
`DispatchResult::Error`, then inspect the kind (`RunErrorKind::App` or
`RunErrorKind::External`), `error.exit_status()`, and `error.as_str()`. See
[Execution Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md) and [Testing](./testing.md).

1	# Output Modes
2	
3	Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.
4	
5	The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.
6	
7	## The OutputMode Enum
8	
9	```rust
10	pub enum OutputMode {
11	    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
12	    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
13	    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
14	    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
15	    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
16	    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
17	    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
18	    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
19	}
20	```
21	
22	Three categories:
23	
24	**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.
25	
26	**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.
27	
28	**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.
29	
30	## Auto Mode
31	
32	`Auto` is the default when `--output` is absent, and an application can change
33	that default with
34	[`output_mode_fallback(mode)`](./app-configuration.md#output-mode-fallback) — an
35	explicit `--output` still outranks it. `Auto` queries the terminal for color
36	support:
37	
38	```rust
39	Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
40	```
41	
42	If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).
43	
44	This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:
45	
46	```bash
47	myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
48	myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
49	myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
50	```

53	
54	Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:
55	
56	```bash
57	myapp list --output=auto        # Default
58	myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
59	myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
60	myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
61	myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization

63	myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
64	myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
65	```

70	
71	**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
72	when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:
73	
74	```bash
75	myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
76	```
77	
78	Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

81	not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
82	same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
83	is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
84	the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
85	that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
86	`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
87	`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
88	into `term`.

91

97

99	writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
100	those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
101	them itself.
102

104	them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any

106	against `term` or `text`.

109	
110	TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

115	```

120	- Verifying style tag placement

123	Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.

125	style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.
126	
127	## Structured Modes
128

130	
131	```rust
132	#[derive(Serialize)]
133	struct ListOutput {
134	    items: Vec<Item>,
135	    total: usize,
136	}
137	
138	fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
139	    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
140	}
141	```
142	
143	```bash
144	myapp list --output=json
145	```
146	
147	```json

149	  "items": [...],
150	  "total": 42
151	}
152	```

154	Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:

157	- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
158	- API-like behavior from CLI apps

161

169	```rust
170	use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
171	use standout::OutputMode;
172	use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;
173	
174	let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
175	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
176	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
177	    .build();
178	
179	render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
180	```
181	
182	The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).
183	
184	When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
185	attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:
186	
187	```rust
188	use serde_json::json;
189	use standout::cli::FnHandler;
190	use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
191	use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};
192	
193	let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
194	    CsvProjection::builder("items")
195	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
196	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
197	        .derived_column(
198	            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
199	            |row, _root| json!(
200	                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
201	                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
202	            ),
203	        )
204	        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
205	            "language": "TOTAL",
206	            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
207	            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
208	        }))
209	        .conditional_row(|root| {
210	            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
211	                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
212	        })
213	        .build(),
214	);
215	
216	App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
217	    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
218	})?;
219	```

222	columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
223	callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column

226	The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the

# Output Modes

Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.

The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.

## The OutputMode Enum

```rust
pub enum OutputMode {
    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
}
```

Three categories:

**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.

**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.

**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.

## Auto Mode

`Auto` is the default when `--output` is absent, and an application can change
that default with
[`output_mode_fallback(mode)`](./app-configuration.md#output-mode-fallback) — an
explicit `--output` still outranks it. `Auto` queries the terminal for color
support:

```rust
Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
```

If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).

This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:

```bash
myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
```

## The --output Flag

Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:

```bash
myapp list --output=auto        # Default
myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
```

The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.

## Term vs Text

**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:

```bash
myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
```

Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
into `term`.

**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:

```bash
myapp list --output=text
```

Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.

Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
them itself.

`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
against `term` or `text`.

## TermDebug Mode

TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

```text
Template: [title]Hello[/title]
Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
```

Use cases:

- Debugging template issues
- Verifying style tag placement
- Automated testing of template output

Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.

## Structured Modes

Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListOutput {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
}
```

```bash
myapp list --output=json
```

```json
{
  "items": [...],
  "total": 42
}
```

Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:

- Machine-readable output for scripts
- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
- API-like behavior from CLI apps

### CSV Output

Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.

The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
a caller needs explicit columns and headers:

```rust
use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
use standout::OutputMode;
use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;

let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
    .build();

render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
```

The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).

When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:

```rust
use serde_json::json;
use standout::cli::FnHandler;
use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};

let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
    CsvProjection::builder("items")
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
        .derived_column(
            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
            |row, _root| json!(
                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
            ),
        )
        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
            "language": "TOTAL",
            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
        }))
        .conditional_row(|root| {
            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
        })
        .build(),
);

App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
})?;
```

Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.

The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
therefore all observe the same projected CSV.

See [Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for
tabular specifications and layout.

## File Output

The `--output-file-path` flag redirects output to a file:

```bash
myapp list --output-file-path=results.txt
myapp list --output=json --output-file-path=data.json
```

Behavior:

- Text output: written to file, nothing printed to stdout
- Binary output: written to the requested file instead of stdout
- Silent output: no-op

After writing to file, stdout output is suppressed to prevent double-printing.

## Customizing Flags

Rename or disable the flags via `AppBuilder`:

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_flag(Some("format"))       // --format instead of --output
    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))     // --out instead of --output-file-path
    .build()?
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_flag()                  // Disable --output entirely
    .no_output_file_flag()             // Disable file output
    .build()?
```

## Keep Output Mode Out of Handlers

Output mode is a rendering concern and is deliberately absent from
`CommandContext`. A handler should return the same serializable data regardless
of whether the caller selected terminal, text, or structured output. If a
command's behavior genuinely differs, model that as an explicit command or
argument rather than an implicit presentation-mode branch.

## Rendering Without CLI

For standalone rendering with explicit mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_auto, OutputMode};

// Renders template for Term/Text, serializes for Json/Yaml
let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
```

The "auto" in `render_auto` refers to template-vs-serialize dispatch, not color detection.

For full control over both output mode and color mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_with_mode, ColorMode};

let output = render_with_mode(
    template,
    &data,
    &theme,
    OutputMode::Term,
    ColorMode::Dark,
)?;
```
