1	# Introduction to Tabular
2	
3	Polished terminal output requires two things: good formatting (see [Rendering Introduction](intro-to-rendering.md)) and good layouts. For text-only, non-interactive output, layout mostly means aligning things vertically and controlling how multiple pieces of information are presented together.
4	
5	Tabular provides a declarative column system with powerful primitives for sizing (fixed, range, fill, fractions), positioning (anchor to right), overflow handling (clip, wrap, truncate), cell alignment, and automated per-column styling.
6	
7	Tabular is not only about tables. Any listing where items have multiple fields that benefit from vertical alignment is a good candidate—log entries with authors, timestamps, and messages; file listings with names, sizes, and dates; task lists with IDs, titles, and statuses. Add headers, separators, and borders to a tabular layout, and you have a table.
8	
9	**Key capabilities:**
10	
11	- **Flexible sizing**: Fixed widths, min/max ranges, fill remaining space, fractional proportions
12	- **Smart truncation**: Truncate at start, middle, or end with custom ellipsis
13	- **Word wrapping**: Wrap long content across multiple lines with proper alignment
14	- **Unicode-aware**: CJK characters, combining marks, and ANSI codes handled correctly
15	- **Dynamic styling**: Style columns or individual values based on content
16	
17	In this guide, we will walk from a simple listing to a polished table, exploring the available features.
18	
19	**See Also:**
20	
21	- [Introduction to Rendering](intro-to-rendering.md) - templates and styles overview
22	- [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) - themes and adaptive styles
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Our Example: Task List
27	
28	We'll build the output for a task list. This is a perfect Tabular use case: each task has an index, title, and status. We want them aligned, readable, and visually clear at a glance.
29	
30	Here's our data:
31	
32	```rust
33	use serde::Serialize;
34	
35	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
36	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
37	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
38	
39	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
40	struct Task {
41	    title: String,
42	    status: Status,
43	}
44	
45	let tasks = vec![
46	    Task { title: "Implement user authentication".into(), status: Status::Pending },
47	    Task { title: "Fix payment gateway timeout".into(), status: Status::Pending },
48	    Task { title: "Update documentation for API v2".into(), status: Status::Done },
49	    Task { title: "Review pull request #142".into(), status: Status::Pending },
50	];
51	```
52	
53	Let's progressively build this from raw output to a polished, professional listing.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## Step 1: The Problem with Plain Output
58	
59	Without any formatting, a naive approach might look like this:
60	
61	```jinja
62	{% for task in tasks %}
63	{{ loop.index }}. {{ task.title }} {{ task.status }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	Output:
68	
69	```text
70	1. Implement user authentication pending
71	2. Fix payment gateway timeout pending
72	3. Update documentation for API v2 done
73	4. Review pull request #142 pending
74	```
75	
76	This is barely readable. Fields run together, nothing aligns, and scanning the list requires mental parsing of each line. Let's fix that.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## Step 2: Basic Column Alignment with `col`
81	
82	The simplest improvement is the `col` filter. It pads (or truncates) each value to a fixed width:
83	
84	```jinja
85	{% for task in tasks %}
86	{{ loop.index | col(4) }}  {{ task.status | col(10) }}  {{ task.title | col(40) }}
87	{% endfor %}
88	```
89	
90	Output:
91	
92	```text
93	1.    pending     Implement user authentication
94	2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
95	3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
96	4.    pending     Review pull request #142
97	```
98	
99	Already much better. Each column aligns vertically, making it easy to scan. But we've hardcoded widths, and if a title is too long, it gets truncated with `...`.
100	
101	> **Key insight:** The `col` filter handles Unicode correctly. CJK characters count as 2 columns, combining marks don't add width, and ANSI escape codes are preserved but not counted.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## Step 3: Structured Layout with `tabular()`
106	
107	For more control, use the `tabular()` function. This creates a formatter that you configure once and use for all rows:
108	
109	```jinja
110	{% set t = tabular([
111	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
112	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
113	    {"name": "title", "width": 40}
114	], separator="  ") %}
115	
116	{% for task in tasks %}
117	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
118	{% endfor %}
119	```
120	
121	The output looks the same, but now the column definitions are centralized. This becomes powerful when we start adding features.
122	
123	---
124	
125	## Step 4: Flexible Widths
126	
127	Hardcoded widths are fragile. What if the terminal is wider or narrower? Tabular offers flexible width strategies:
128	
129	| Width | Meaning |
130	| ----- | ------- |
131	| `8` | Exactly 8 columns (fixed) |
132	| `{"min": 10}` | At least 10 columns, and as wide as the widest cell when you pass `rows=` |
133	| `{"min": 10, "max": 30}` | Between 10 and 30, alongside a `"fill"` column |
134	| `"fill"` | Takes all remaining space |
135	| `"2fr"` | 2 parts of remaining (proportional) |
136	
137	A `{"min": ..., "max": ...}` column is resolved once, when `tabular()` or
138	`table()` builds the formatter. The formatter then formats one row at a time,
139	so it can only measure content it was handed up front: pass the rows you are
140	about to render as `rows=`, and every bounded column is sized to its widest
141	cell (still clamped by `max`) before the first row is formatted.
142	
143	`rows=` takes an array of row arrays — the same cells `.row(...)` takes — so
144	hand it the list you are about to loop over:
145	
146	```jinja
147	{% set t = tabular([
148	    {"width": {"min": 0}},
149	    {"width": {"min": 0}},
150	    {"width": "fill"}
151	], separator="  ", rows=rows) %}
152	
153	{% for row in rows %}
154	{{ t.row(row) }}
155	{% endfor %}
156	```
157	
158	with `rows` a list of `[index, status, title]` arrays from the handler's data.
159	`table()` takes the same `rows=`, and measures its `header=` row alongside the
160	data so a header wider than its column is not truncated. A row — or a `header=`
161	— shorter than the column list measures the columns it leaves out at their
162	`null_repr`, the text the formatter renders there. A column carrying
163	`sub_columns` is not measured from `rows=`, because its sub-columns are
164	resolved per row against the parent's width (see Step 7).
165	
166	Without `rows=` a bounded column has nothing to grow it: it lands on its `min`,
167	and with no `"fill"` (or fractional) column in the table any leftover terminal
168	width is added to the rightmost bounded column instead, regardless of its
169	`max`.
170	
171	Let's make the title column expand to fill available space:
172	
173	```jinja
174	{% set t = tabular([
175	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
176	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
177	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
178	], separator="  ") %}
179	```
180	
181	Now on an 80-column terminal:
182	
183	```text
184	1.    pending     Implement user authentication
185	2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
186	3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
187	4.    pending     Review pull request #142
188	```
189	
190	On a 120-column terminal, the title column automatically expands to use the extra space.
191	
192	The layout adapts to the available space.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Step 5: Right-Align Numbers
197	
198	Numbers and indices look better right-aligned. Use the `align` option:
199	
200	```jinja
201	{% set t = tabular([
202	    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "align": "right"},
203	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
204	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
205	], separator="  ") %}
206	```
207	
208	Output:
209	
210	```text
211	  1.  pending     Implement user authentication
212	  2.  pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
213	  3.  done        Update documentation for API v2
214	  4.  pending     Review pull request #142
215	```
216	
217	The indices now align on the right edge of their column.
218	
219	---
220	
221	## Step 6: Anchoring Columns
222	
223	Sometimes you want a column pinned to the terminal's right edge, regardless of how other columns resize. Use `anchor`:
224	
225	```jinja
226	{% set t = tabular([
227	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
228	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
229	    {"name": "status", "width": 10, "anchor": "right"}
230	], separator="  ") %}
231	```
232	
233	Now the status column is always at the right edge. If the terminal is 100 columns or 200, the status stays anchored. The fill column absorbs the extra space between fixed columns and anchored columns.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## Step 7: Sub-Columns (Distributing Space Within a Column)
238	
239	Sometimes a column contains multiple logical parts with different sizing needs. A common example: a task list where the middle column has a variable-length title and an optional tag, separated by flexible spacing.
240	
241	Without sub-columns, you can't compose `title + padding + tag` because the caller doesn't know the resolved column width. Sub-columns solve this by letting you define inner structure that is resolved per-row within the parent column's width.
242	
243	### The Problem
244	
245	Consider this layout with three columns: index (fixed), content (fill), and duration (fixed right-aligned). The content column should contain a title that grows and an optional tag that's right-aligned:
246	
247	```text
248	1.  Gallery Navigation              [feature]  4d
249	2.  Bug : Static Analysis                      8h
250	3.  Fixing Layout of Image Nav      [bug]      2d
251	```
252	
253	The tag `[feature]` must be right-aligned within the content column, with the title filling the remaining space. This is impossible with flat columns because the content column's resolved width isn't known to the template.
254	
255	### The Solution
256	
257	Define `sub_columns` on the parent column. Exactly one sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower); the rest are Fixed or Bounded:
258	
259	```jinja
260	{% set t = tabular([
261	    {"width": 4},
262	    {"width": "fill", "sub_columns": {
263	        "columns": [
264	            {"width": "fill"},
265	            {"width": {"min": 0, "max": 30}, "align": "right"}
266	        ],
267	        "separator": " "
268	    }},
269	    {"width": 4, "align": "right"}
270	], separator="  ", width=60) %}
271	```
272	
273	Now pass nested arrays for the sub-column cells:
274	
275	```jinja
276	{% for task in tasks %}
277	{{ t.row([loop.index ~ ".", [task.title, task.tag], task.duration]) }}
278	{% endfor %}
279	```
280	
281	Each row resolves sub-column widths independently. If the tag is empty (Bounded with min=0), it takes zero width and the title fills the entire column. If the tag is present, it gets its content width (up to max=30) and the title gets the rest.
282	
283	### Sub-Column Options
284	
285	Sub-columns support the same formatting options as regular columns:
286	
287	| Option | Meaning |
288	| ------ | ------- |
289	| `width` | `"fill"`, number (fixed), or `{"min": n, "max": m}` (bounded) |
290	| `align` | `"left"` (default), `"right"`, or `"center"` |
291	| `overflow` | `"truncate"`, `"clip"`, `"wrap"`, or object form |
292	| `style` | Style name to wrap sub-cell content |
293	
294	### Rust API
295	
296	From Rust, use `CellValue::Sub` for sub-column cells:
297	
298	```rust
299	use standout_render::tabular::{
300	    TabularSpec, Col, SubCol, SubColumns, TabularFormatter, CellValue,
301	};
302	
303	let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
304	    .column(Col::fixed(4))
305	    .column(Col::fill().sub_columns(
306	        SubColumns::new(
307	            vec![SubCol::fill(), SubCol::bounded(0, 30).right()],
308	            " ",
309	        ).unwrap(),
310	    ))
311	    .column(Col::fixed(4).align(standout_render::tabular::Align::Right))
312	    .separator("  ")
313	    .build();
314	
315	let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 60);
316	
317	let row = formatter.format_row_cells(&[
318	    CellValue::Single("1."),
319	    CellValue::Sub(vec!["Gallery Navigation", "[feature]"]),
320	    CellValue::Single("4d"),
321	]);
322	```
323	
324	`TabularFormatter::new` uses narrow ambiguous-character widths for backward
325	compatibility. To match terminals where East Asian Ambiguous glyphs occupy two
326	columns, construct the formatter explicitly:
327	
328	```rust
329	use standout_render::AmbiguousWidth;
330	
331	let formatter = TabularFormatter::with_ambiguous_width(
332	    &spec,
333	    60,
334	    AmbiguousWidth::Wide,
335	);
336	```
337	
338	The same policy is used for separators, data-driven width resolution,
339	sub-columns, borders, padding, truncation, and wrapping. MiniJinja `col`,
340	`display_width`, padding, truncation, `tabular`, and `table` operations receive
341	the renderer or application policy automatically.
342	
343	MiniJinja `tabular()` and `table()` also use the terminal width supplied by the
344	current application render context when `width` is omitted. An explicit
345	`width=...` argument takes precedence. The default terminal-width detector
346	consults a valid positive `$COLUMNS` value before probing the terminal. When
347	neither source resolves a width, both helpers use a deterministic 80-column
348	fallback.
349	
350	Policy-aware counterparts are also available for direct construction, including
351	`TabularFormatter::with_widths_and_ambiguous_width`,
352	`TabularFormatter::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`,
353	`Table::from_spec_with_ambiguous_width`, and
354	`Table::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`. Lower-level MiniJinja environments can
355	use `register_tabular_filters_with_policy`.
356	
357	In Wide mode, a decorated Unicode table treats its requested width as a hard
358	maximum. The selected Light, Heavy, Double, or Rounded border is preserved. If
359	an odd width cannot be filled by a two-column horizontal border glyph, that
360	border row may underfill by one column; it never exceeds the maximum or silently
361	switches to ASCII. Narrow table geometry is unchanged.
362	
363	### Design Constraints
364	
365	- **One level only**: Sub-columns cannot be nested recursively.
366	- **Exactly one Fill**: One sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower). The rest must be Fixed or Bounded.
367	- **Per-row resolution**: Sub-column widths are computed independently for each row, based on actual content.
368	- **Width invariant**: The formatted sub-cell output is always exactly the parent column's width.
369	
370	---
371	
372	## Step 8: Handling Long Content
373	
374	What happens when a title is longer than its column? By default, Tabular truncates at the end with `...`. But you have options:
375	
376	### Truncate at Different Positions
377	
378	```jinja
379	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": "truncate"}                        {# "Very long title th..." #}
380	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "start"}}}     {# "...itle that is long" #}
381	{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}    {# "Very long...is long" #}
382	```
383	
384	Middle truncation is perfect for file paths where both the start and end matter: `/home/user/.../important.txt`
385	
386	Semantic style tags are zero-width layout metadata. Tabular measures only the
387	visible characters, and truncation preserves balanced tags around retained
388	text. For example, truncating `prefix [match]needle[/match] suffix` at 12
389	columns produces `prefix [match]need[/match]…`; the highlighted portion remains
390	styled when rendered. Plain-text output is the only stage that strips tags.
391	
392	### Wrap to Multiple Lines
393	
394	For descriptions or messages, wrapping is often better than truncating:
395	
396	```jinja
397	{% set t = tabular([
398	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
399	    {"name": "title", "width": 40, "overflow": "wrap"},
400	    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
401	], separator="  ") %}
402	```
403	
404	If a title exceeds 40 columns, it wraps:
405	
406	```text
407	1.    Implement comprehensive error handling    pending
408	      for all API endpoints with proper
409	      logging and user feedback
410	2.    Quick fix                                 done
411	```
412	
413	The wrapped lines are indented to align with the column.
414	
415	---
416	
417	## Step 9: Dynamic Styling Based on Values
418	
419	Here's where Tabular shines for task lists. We want status colors: green for done, yellow for pending.
420	
421	First, define styles in your theme:
422	
423	```css
424	/* styles/default.css */
425	.done { color: green; }
426	.pending { color: yellow; }
427	```
428	
429	Then use the `style_as` filter to apply styles based on the value itself:
430	
431	```jinja
432	{% set t = tabular([
433	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
434	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
435	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
436	], separator="  ") %}
437	
438	{% for task in tasks %}
439	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
440	{% endfor %}
441	```
442	
443	The `style_as` filter wraps the value in style tags: `[done]done[/done]`. The rendering system then applies the green color.
444	
445	Output (with colors):
446	
447	```text
448	1.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Implement user authentication
449	2.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Fix payment gateway timeout
450	3.    [green]done[/green]        Update documentation for API v2
451	4.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Review pull request #142
452	```
453	
454	In the terminal, statuses appear in their respective colors, making it instantly clear which tasks need attention.
455	
456	---
457	
458	## Step 10: Column-Level Styles
459	
460	Instead of styling individual values, you can style entire columns. This is useful for de-emphasizing certain information:
461	
462	```jinja
463	{% set t = tabular([
464	    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
465	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
466	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
467	], separator="  ") %}
468	```
469	
470	Now indices appear in a muted style (typically gray), while titles and statuses remain prominent. This creates visual hierarchy.
471	
472	---
473	
474	## Step 11: Automatic Field Extraction
475	
476	Tired of manually listing `[task.title, task.status, ...]`? If your column names match your struct fields, use `row_from()`:
477	
478	```jinja
479	{% set t = tabular([
480	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
481	    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
482	]) %}
483	
484	{% for task in tasks %}
485	{{ t.row_from(task) }}
486	{% endfor %}
487	```
488	
489	Tabular extracts `task.title`, `task.status`, etc. automatically. For nested fields, use `key`:
490	
491	```jinja
492	{"name": "Author", "key": "author.name", "width": 20}
493	{"name": "Email", "key": "author.email", "width": 30}
494	```
495	
496	---
497	
498	## Step 12: Adding Headers and Borders
499	
500	For a proper table with headers, switch from `tabular()` to `table()`:
501	
502	```jinja
503	{% set t = table([
504	    {"name": "#", "width": 4},
505	    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
506	    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill"}
507	], border="rounded", header_style="bold") %}
508	
509	{{ t.header_row() }}
510	{{ t.separator_row() }}
511	{% for task in tasks %}
512	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
513	{% endfor %}
514	{{ t.bottom_border() }}
515	```
516	
517	Output:
518	
519	```text
520	╭──────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────╮
521	│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                  │
522	├──────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
523	│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication          │
524	│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout            │
525	│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2        │
526	│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142               │
527	╰──────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────╯
528	```
529	
530	### Border Styles
531	
532	Choose from six border styles:
533	
534	| Style | Look |
535	| ----- | ---- |
536	| `"none"` | No borders |
537	| `"ascii"` | `+--+--+` (ASCII compatible) |
538	| `"light"` | `┌──┬──┐` |
539	| `"heavy"` | `┏━━┳━━┓` |
540	| `"double"` | `╔══╦══╗` |
541	| `"rounded"` | `╭──┬──╮` |
542	
543	### Row Separators
544	
545	For dense data, add lines between rows:
546	
547	```jinja
548	{% set t = table(columns, border="light", row_separator=true) %}
549	```
550	
551	```text
552	┌──────┬────────────────────────────────────╮
553	│ #    │ Title                              │
554	├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
555	│ 1    │ Implement user authentication      │
556	├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
557	│ 2    │ Fix payment gateway timeout        │
558	└──────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
559	```
560	
561	### Alternating Row Styles
562	
563	For long tables, alternating background colors on even/odd rows improves readability (sometimes called "zebra striping"). Pass `row_styles` to the `table()` function:
564	
565	```jinja
566	{# Default gray tint — subtle dark/light gray alternation #}
567	{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles=true) %}
568	
569	{# Named tint — blue, red, green, or purple #}
570	{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles="blue") %}
571	
572	{# Fully custom style names #}
573	{% set t = table(columns, row_styles=["my_even", "my_odd"]) %}
574	```
575	
576	The default theme includes five adaptive tints that automatically adjust to the user's light/dark terminal setting:
577	
578	| Tint | Usage | Dark mode | Light mode |
579	| -------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------ |
580	| gray | `row_styles=true` | dark gray bg | light gray bg |
581	| blue | `row_styles="blue"` | dark navy bg | lavender bg |
582	| red | `row_styles="red"` | dark crimson bg | blush bg |
583	| green | `row_styles="green"` | dark forest bg | mint bg |
584	| purple | `row_styles="purple"` | dark plum bg | lilac bg |
585	
586	The Rust API equivalent is `Table::row_styles("table_row_even", "table_row_odd")`.
587	
588	---
589	
590	## Step 13: The Complete Example
591	
592	Putting it all together, here's a polished task list:
593	
594	```jinja
595	{% set t = table([
596	    {"name": "#", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
597	    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
598	    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill", "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}
599	], border="rounded", header_style="bold", separator=" | ") %}
600	
601	{{ t.header_row() }}
602	{{ t.separator_row() }}
603	{% for task in tasks %}
604	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
605	{% endfor %}
606	{{ t.bottom_border() }}
607	```
608	
609	Output (80 columns, with styling):
610	
611	```text
612	╭──────┬────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
613	│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                                 │
614	├──────┼────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
615	│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication                         │
616	│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout                           │
617	│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2                       │
618	│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142                              │
619	╰──────┴────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
620	```
621	
622	Features in use:
623	
624	- **Rounded borders** for a modern look
625	- **Muted styling** on index column for visual hierarchy
626	- **Fill width** on title to use available space
627	- **Middle truncation** for titles that exceed the column
628	- **Dynamic status colors** via `style_as`
629	
630	---
631	
632	## Using Tabular from Rust
633	
634	Everything shown in templates is also available in Rust:
635	
636	```rust
637	use standout_render::tabular::{Col, TabularFormatter, TabularSpec};
638	
639	let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
640	    .column(Col::fixed(4).header("#").style("muted"))
641	    .column(Col::fixed(10).header("Status"))
642	    .column(Col::fill().header("Title").truncate_middle())
643	    .separator(" | ")
644	    .build();
645	
646	let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 80);
647	
648	// Format individual rows
649	for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate() {
650	    let row = formatter.format_row(&[
651	        &(i + 1).to_string(),
652	        &task.status.to_string(),
653	        &task.title,
654	    ]);
655	    println!("{}", row);
656	}
657	```
658	
659	---
660	
661	## Summary
662	
663	Tabular transforms raw data into polished, scannable output with minimal effort:
664	
665	1. **Start simple** - use `col` filter for quick alignment
666	2. **Structure with `tabular()`** - centralize column definitions
667	3. **Flex with widths** - use `fill`, bounded ranges, and fractions
668	4. **Align content** - right-align numbers and dates
669	5. **Anchor columns** - pin important data to edges
670	6. **Handle overflow** - truncate intelligently or wrap
671	7. **Add visual hierarchy** - style columns and values dynamically
672	8. **Extract automatically** - let `row_from()` pull fields from structs
673	9. **Decorate as tables** - add borders, headers, and separators
674	
675	The declarative approach means your layout adapts to terminal width, applies the explicitly selected Unicode ambiguous-width policy consistently, and remains maintainable as your data evolves.
676	
677	For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-render).
678

# Introduction to Tabular

Polished terminal output requires two things: good formatting (see [Rendering Introduction](intro-to-rendering.md)) and good layouts. For text-only, non-interactive output, layout mostly means aligning things vertically and controlling how multiple pieces of information are presented together.

Tabular provides a declarative column system with powerful primitives for sizing (fixed, range, fill, fractions), positioning (anchor to right), overflow handling (clip, wrap, truncate), cell alignment, and automated per-column styling.

Tabular is not only about tables. Any listing where items have multiple fields that benefit from vertical alignment is a good candidate—log entries with authors, timestamps, and messages; file listings with names, sizes, and dates; task lists with IDs, titles, and statuses. Add headers, separators, and borders to a tabular layout, and you have a table.

**Key capabilities:**

- **Flexible sizing**: Fixed widths, min/max ranges, fill remaining space, fractional proportions
- **Smart truncation**: Truncate at start, middle, or end with custom ellipsis
- **Word wrapping**: Wrap long content across multiple lines with proper alignment
- **Unicode-aware**: CJK characters, combining marks, and ANSI codes handled correctly
- **Dynamic styling**: Style columns or individual values based on content

In this guide, we will walk from a simple listing to a polished table, exploring the available features.

**See Also:**

- [Introduction to Rendering](intro-to-rendering.md) - templates and styles overview
- [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) - themes and adaptive styles

---

## Our Example: Task List

We'll build the output for a task list. This is a perfect Tabular use case: each task has an index, title, and status. We want them aligned, readable, and visually clear at a glance.

Here's our data:

```rust
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
pub enum Status { Pending, Done }

#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
struct Task {
    title: String,
    status: Status,
}

let tasks = vec![
    Task { title: "Implement user authentication".into(), status: Status::Pending },
    Task { title: "Fix payment gateway timeout".into(), status: Status::Pending },
    Task { title: "Update documentation for API v2".into(), status: Status::Done },
    Task { title: "Review pull request #142".into(), status: Status::Pending },
];
```

Let's progressively build this from raw output to a polished, professional listing.

---

## Step 1: The Problem with Plain Output

Without any formatting, a naive approach might look like this:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ loop.index }}. {{ task.title }} {{ task.status }}
{% endfor %}
```

Output:

```text
1. Implement user authentication pending
2. Fix payment gateway timeout pending
3. Update documentation for API v2 done
4. Review pull request #142 pending
```

This is barely readable. Fields run together, nothing aligns, and scanning the list requires mental parsing of each line. Let's fix that.

---

## Step 2: Basic Column Alignment with `col`

The simplest improvement is the `col` filter. It pads (or truncates) each value to a fixed width:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ loop.index | col(4) }}  {{ task.status | col(10) }}  {{ task.title | col(40) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Output:

```text
1.    pending     Implement user authentication
2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
4.    pending     Review pull request #142
```

Already much better. Each column aligns vertically, making it easy to scan. But we've hardcoded widths, and if a title is too long, it gets truncated with `...`.

> **Key insight:** The `col` filter handles Unicode correctly. CJK characters count as 2 columns, combining marks don't add width, and ANSI escape codes are preserved but not counted.

---

## Step 3: Structured Layout with `tabular()`

For more control, use the `tabular()` function. This creates a formatter that you configure once and use for all rows:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": 40}
], separator="  ") %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

The output looks the same, but now the column definitions are centralized. This becomes powerful when we start adding features.

---

## Step 4: Flexible Widths

Hardcoded widths are fragile. What if the terminal is wider or narrower? Tabular offers flexible width strategies:

| Width | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| `8` | Exactly 8 columns (fixed) |
| `{"min": 10}` | At least 10 columns, and as wide as the widest cell when you pass `rows=` |
| `{"min": 10, "max": 30}` | Between 10 and 30, alongside a `"fill"` column |
| `"fill"` | Takes all remaining space |
| `"2fr"` | 2 parts of remaining (proportional) |

A `{"min": ..., "max": ...}` column is resolved once, when `tabular()` or
`table()` builds the formatter. The formatter then formats one row at a time,
so it can only measure content it was handed up front: pass the rows you are
about to render as `rows=`, and every bounded column is sized to its widest
cell (still clamped by `max`) before the first row is formatted.

`rows=` takes an array of row arrays — the same cells `.row(...)` takes — so
hand it the list you are about to loop over:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"width": {"min": 0}},
    {"width": {"min": 0}},
    {"width": "fill"}
], separator="  ", rows=rows) %}

{% for row in rows %}
{{ t.row(row) }}
{% endfor %}
```

with `rows` a list of `[index, status, title]` arrays from the handler's data.
`table()` takes the same `rows=`, and measures its `header=` row alongside the
data so a header wider than its column is not truncated. A row — or a `header=`
— shorter than the column list measures the columns it leaves out at their
`null_repr`, the text the formatter renders there. A column carrying
`sub_columns` is not measured from `rows=`, because its sub-columns are
resolved per row against the parent's width (see Step 7).

Without `rows=` a bounded column has nothing to grow it: it lands on its `min`,
and with no `"fill"` (or fractional) column in the table any leftover terminal
width is added to the rightmost bounded column instead, regardless of its
`max`.

Let's make the title column expand to fill available space:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now on an 80-column terminal:

```text
1.    pending     Implement user authentication
2.    pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    done        Update documentation for API v2
4.    pending     Review pull request #142
```

On a 120-column terminal, the title column automatically expands to use the extra space.

The layout adapts to the available space.

---

## Step 5: Right-Align Numbers

Numbers and indices look better right-aligned. Use the `align` option:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "align": "right"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Output:

```text
  1.  pending     Implement user authentication
  2.  pending     Fix payment gateway timeout
  3.  done        Update documentation for API v2
  4.  pending     Review pull request #142
```

The indices now align on the right edge of their column.

---

## Step 6: Anchoring Columns

Sometimes you want a column pinned to the terminal's right edge, regardless of how other columns resize. Use `anchor`:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10, "anchor": "right"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now the status column is always at the right edge. If the terminal is 100 columns or 200, the status stays anchored. The fill column absorbs the extra space between fixed columns and anchored columns.

---

## Step 7: Sub-Columns (Distributing Space Within a Column)

Sometimes a column contains multiple logical parts with different sizing needs. A common example: a task list where the middle column has a variable-length title and an optional tag, separated by flexible spacing.

Without sub-columns, you can't compose `title + padding + tag` because the caller doesn't know the resolved column width. Sub-columns solve this by letting you define inner structure that is resolved per-row within the parent column's width.

### The Problem

Consider this layout with three columns: index (fixed), content (fill), and duration (fixed right-aligned). The content column should contain a title that grows and an optional tag that's right-aligned:

```text
1.  Gallery Navigation              [feature]  4d
2.  Bug : Static Analysis                      8h
3.  Fixing Layout of Image Nav      [bug]      2d
```

The tag `[feature]` must be right-aligned within the content column, with the title filling the remaining space. This is impossible with flat columns because the content column's resolved width isn't known to the template.

### The Solution

Define `sub_columns` on the parent column. Exactly one sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower); the rest are Fixed or Bounded:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"width": 4},
    {"width": "fill", "sub_columns": {
        "columns": [
            {"width": "fill"},
            {"width": {"min": 0, "max": 30}, "align": "right"}
        ],
        "separator": " "
    }},
    {"width": 4, "align": "right"}
], separator="  ", width=60) %}
```

Now pass nested arrays for the sub-column cells:

```jinja
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index ~ ".", [task.title, task.tag], task.duration]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Each row resolves sub-column widths independently. If the tag is empty (Bounded with min=0), it takes zero width and the title fills the entire column. If the tag is present, it gets its content width (up to max=30) and the title gets the rest.

### Sub-Column Options

Sub-columns support the same formatting options as regular columns:

| Option | Meaning |
| ------ | ------- |
| `width` | `"fill"`, number (fixed), or `{"min": n, "max": m}` (bounded) |
| `align` | `"left"` (default), `"right"`, or `"center"` |
| `overflow` | `"truncate"`, `"clip"`, `"wrap"`, or object form |
| `style` | Style name to wrap sub-cell content |

### Rust API

From Rust, use `CellValue::Sub` for sub-column cells:

```rust
use standout_render::tabular::{
    TabularSpec, Col, SubCol, SubColumns, TabularFormatter, CellValue,
};

let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
    .column(Col::fixed(4))
    .column(Col::fill().sub_columns(
        SubColumns::new(
            vec![SubCol::fill(), SubCol::bounded(0, 30).right()],
            " ",
        ).unwrap(),
    ))
    .column(Col::fixed(4).align(standout_render::tabular::Align::Right))
    .separator("  ")
    .build();

let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 60);

let row = formatter.format_row_cells(&[
    CellValue::Single("1."),
    CellValue::Sub(vec!["Gallery Navigation", "[feature]"]),
    CellValue::Single("4d"),
]);
```

`TabularFormatter::new` uses narrow ambiguous-character widths for backward
compatibility. To match terminals where East Asian Ambiguous glyphs occupy two
columns, construct the formatter explicitly:

```rust
use standout_render::AmbiguousWidth;

let formatter = TabularFormatter::with_ambiguous_width(
    &spec,
    60,
    AmbiguousWidth::Wide,
);
```

The same policy is used for separators, data-driven width resolution,
sub-columns, borders, padding, truncation, and wrapping. MiniJinja `col`,
`display_width`, padding, truncation, `tabular`, and `table` operations receive
the renderer or application policy automatically.

MiniJinja `tabular()` and `table()` also use the terminal width supplied by the
current application render context when `width` is omitted. An explicit
`width=...` argument takes precedence. The default terminal-width detector
consults a valid positive `$COLUMNS` value before probing the terminal. When
neither source resolves a width, both helpers use a deterministic 80-column
fallback.

Policy-aware counterparts are also available for direct construction, including
`TabularFormatter::with_widths_and_ambiguous_width`,
`TabularFormatter::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`,
`Table::from_spec_with_ambiguous_width`, and
`Table::from_type_with_ambiguous_width`. Lower-level MiniJinja environments can
use `register_tabular_filters_with_policy`.

In Wide mode, a decorated Unicode table treats its requested width as a hard
maximum. The selected Light, Heavy, Double, or Rounded border is preserved. If
an odd width cannot be filled by a two-column horizontal border glyph, that
border row may underfill by one column; it never exceeds the maximum or silently
switches to ASCII. Narrow table geometry is unchanged.

### Design Constraints

- **One level only**: Sub-columns cannot be nested recursively.
- **Exactly one Fill**: One sub-column must be `"fill"` (the grower). The rest must be Fixed or Bounded.
- **Per-row resolution**: Sub-column widths are computed independently for each row, based on actual content.
- **Width invariant**: The formatted sub-cell output is always exactly the parent column's width.

---

## Step 8: Handling Long Content

What happens when a title is longer than its column? By default, Tabular truncates at the end with `...`. But you have options:

### Truncate at Different Positions

```jinja
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": "truncate"}                        {# "Very long title th..." #}
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "start"}}}     {# "...itle that is long" #}
{"name": "title", "width": 30, "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}    {# "Very long...is long" #}
```

Middle truncation is perfect for file paths where both the start and end matter: `/home/user/.../important.txt`

Semantic style tags are zero-width layout metadata. Tabular measures only the
visible characters, and truncation preserves balanced tags around retained
text. For example, truncating `prefix [match]needle[/match] suffix` at 12
columns produces `prefix [match]need[/match]…`; the highlighted portion remains
styled when rendered. Plain-text output is the only stage that strips tags.

### Wrap to Multiple Lines

For descriptions or messages, wrapping is often better than truncating:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "title", "width": 40, "overflow": "wrap"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
], separator="  ") %}
```

If a title exceeds 40 columns, it wraps:

```text
1.    Implement comprehensive error handling    pending
      for all API endpoints with proper
      logging and user feedback
2.    Quick fix                                 done
```

The wrapped lines are indented to align with the column.

---

## Step 9: Dynamic Styling Based on Values

Here's where Tabular shines for task lists. We want status colors: green for done, yellow for pending.

First, define styles in your theme:

```css
/* styles/default.css */
.done { color: green; }
.pending { color: yellow; }
```

Then use the `style_as` filter to apply styles based on the value itself:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
```

The `style_as` filter wraps the value in style tags: `[done]done[/done]`. The rendering system then applies the green color.

Output (with colors):

```text
1.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Implement user authentication
2.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Fix payment gateway timeout
3.    [green]done[/green]        Update documentation for API v2
4.    [yellow]pending[/yellow]   Review pull request #142
```

In the terminal, statuses appear in their respective colors, making it instantly clear which tasks need attention.

---

## Step 10: Column-Level Styles

Instead of styling individual values, you can style entire columns. This is useful for de-emphasizing certain information:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "index", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
], separator="  ") %}
```

Now indices appear in a muted style (typically gray), while titles and statuses remain prominent. This creates visual hierarchy.

---

## Step 11: Automatic Field Extraction

Tired of manually listing `[task.title, task.status, ...]`? If your column names match your struct fields, use `row_from()`:

```jinja
{% set t = tabular([
    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"},
    {"name": "status", "width": 10}
]) %}

{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row_from(task) }}
{% endfor %}
```

Tabular extracts `task.title`, `task.status`, etc. automatically. For nested fields, use `key`:

```jinja
{"name": "Author", "key": "author.name", "width": 20}
{"name": "Email", "key": "author.email", "width": 30}
```

---

## Step 12: Adding Headers and Borders

For a proper table with headers, switch from `tabular()` to `table()`:

```jinja
{% set t = table([
    {"name": "#", "width": 4},
    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill"}
], border="rounded", header_style="bold") %}

{{ t.header_row() }}
{{ t.separator_row() }}
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status, task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
{{ t.bottom_border() }}
```

Output:

```text
╭──────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                  │
├──────┼────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication          │
│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout            │
│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2        │
│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142               │
╰──────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

### Border Styles

Choose from six border styles:

| Style | Look |
| ----- | ---- |
| `"none"` | No borders |
| `"ascii"` | `+--+--+` (ASCII compatible) |
| `"light"` | `┌──┬──┐` |
| `"heavy"` | `┏━━┳━━┓` |
| `"double"` | `╔══╦══╗` |
| `"rounded"` | `╭──┬──╮` |

### Row Separators

For dense data, add lines between rows:

```jinja
{% set t = table(columns, border="light", row_separator=true) %}
```

```text
┌──────┬────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Title                              │
├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ Implement user authentication      │
├──────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2    │ Fix payment gateway timeout        │
└──────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Alternating Row Styles

For long tables, alternating background colors on even/odd rows improves readability (sometimes called "zebra striping"). Pass `row_styles` to the `table()` function:

```jinja
{# Default gray tint — subtle dark/light gray alternation #}
{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles=true) %}

{# Named tint — blue, red, green, or purple #}
{% set t = table(columns, header_style="bold", row_styles="blue") %}

{# Fully custom style names #}
{% set t = table(columns, row_styles=["my_even", "my_odd"]) %}
```

The default theme includes five adaptive tints that automatically adjust to the user's light/dark terminal setting:

| Tint | Usage | Dark mode | Light mode |
| -------- | ------- | ----------- | ------------ |
| gray | `row_styles=true` | dark gray bg | light gray bg |
| blue | `row_styles="blue"` | dark navy bg | lavender bg |
| red | `row_styles="red"` | dark crimson bg | blush bg |
| green | `row_styles="green"` | dark forest bg | mint bg |
| purple | `row_styles="purple"` | dark plum bg | lilac bg |

The Rust API equivalent is `Table::row_styles("table_row_even", "table_row_odd")`.

---

## Step 13: The Complete Example

Putting it all together, here's a polished task list:

```jinja
{% set t = table([
    {"name": "#", "width": 4, "style": "muted"},
    {"name": "Status", "width": 10},
    {"name": "Title", "width": "fill", "overflow": {"truncate": {"at": "middle"}}}
], border="rounded", header_style="bold", separator=" | ") %}

{{ t.header_row() }}
{{ t.separator_row() }}
{% for task in tasks %}
{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
{% endfor %}
{{ t.bottom_border() }}
```

Output (80 columns, with styling):

```text
╭──────┬────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ #    │ Status     │ Title                                                 │
├──────┼────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1    │ pending    │ Implement user authentication                         │
│ 2    │ pending    │ Fix payment gateway timeout                           │
│ 3    │ done       │ Update documentation for API v2                       │
│ 4    │ pending    │ Review pull request #142                              │
╰──────┴────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

Features in use:

- **Rounded borders** for a modern look
- **Muted styling** on index column for visual hierarchy
- **Fill width** on title to use available space
- **Middle truncation** for titles that exceed the column
- **Dynamic status colors** via `style_as`

---

## Using Tabular from Rust

Everything shown in templates is also available in Rust:

```rust
use standout_render::tabular::{Col, TabularFormatter, TabularSpec};

let spec = TabularSpec::builder()
    .column(Col::fixed(4).header("#").style("muted"))
    .column(Col::fixed(10).header("Status"))
    .column(Col::fill().header("Title").truncate_middle())
    .separator(" | ")
    .build();

let formatter = TabularFormatter::new(&spec, 80);

// Format individual rows
for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate() {
    let row = formatter.format_row(&[
        &(i + 1).to_string(),
        &task.status.to_string(),
        &task.title,
    ]);
    println!("{}", row);
}
```

---

## Summary

Tabular transforms raw data into polished, scannable output with minimal effort:

1. **Start simple** - use `col` filter for quick alignment
2. **Structure with `tabular()`** - centralize column definitions
3. **Flex with widths** - use `fill`, bounded ranges, and fractions
4. **Align content** - right-align numbers and dates
5. **Anchor columns** - pin important data to edges
6. **Handle overflow** - truncate intelligently or wrap
7. **Add visual hierarchy** - style columns and values dynamically
8. **Extract automatically** - let `row_from()` pull fields from structs
9. **Decorate as tables** - add borders, headers, and separators

The declarative approach means your layout adapts to terminal width, applies the explicitly selected Unicode ambiguous-width policy consistently, and remains maintainable as your data evolves.

For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-render).

1	# Templating
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a two-pass templating system that combines a template engine for logic and data binding with a custom BBCode-like syntax for styling. This separation keeps templates readable while providing full control over both content and presentation.
4	
5	The default engine is MiniJinja (Jinja2-compatible), but alternative engines are available. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for options including a lightweight `SimpleEngine` for reduced binary size.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Two-Pass Rendering Pipeline
10	
11	Templates are processed in two distinct passes:
12	
13	```text
14	Template + Data → [Pass 1: MiniJinja] → Text with style tags → [Pass 2: BBParser] → Final output
15	```
16	
17	**Pass 1 - MiniJinja**: Standard template processing. Variables are substituted, control flow executes, filters apply.
18	
19	**Pass 2 - BBParser**: Style tag processing. Bracket-notation tags are converted to ANSI escape codes (or stripped, depending on output mode).
20	
21	### Pipeline Example
22	
23	```text
24	Template:     [title]{{ name }}[/title] has {{ count }} items
25	Data:         { name: "Report", count: 42 }
26	
27	After Pass 1: [title]Report[/title] has 42 items
28	After Pass 2: \x1b[1;36mReport\x1b[0m has 42 items  (or plain: "Report has 42 items")
29	```
30	
31	This separation means:
32	
33	- Template logic (loops, conditionals) is handled by MiniJinja—a mature, well-documented engine
34	- Style application is a simple, predictable transformation
35	- You can debug each pass independently
36	
37	---
38	
39	## MiniJinja Basics
40	
41	MiniJinja implements Jinja2 syntax, a widely-used templating language. Here's a quick overview:
42	
43	### Variables
44	
45	```jinja
46	{{ variable }}
47	{{ object.field }}
48	{{ list[0] }}
49	```
50	
51	### Control Flow
52	
53	```jinja
54	{% if condition %}
55	  Show this
56	{% elif other_condition %}
57	  Show that
58	{% else %}
59	  Default
60	{% endif %}
61	
62	{% for item in items %}
63	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	### Filters
68	
69	```jinja
70	{{ name | upper }}
71	{{ list | length }}
72	{{ value | default("N/A") }}
73	{{ text | truncate(20) }}
74	```
75	
76	### Comments
77	
78	```jinja
79	{# This is a comment and won't appear in output #}
80	```
81	
82	For comprehensive MiniJinja documentation, see the [MiniJinja documentation](https://docs.rs/minijinja).
83	
84	### Booleans and None
85	
86	Standout renders these the Rust way — `true`, `false`, `none` — not the Jinja2
87	way MiniJinja itself uses (`True`, `False`, `None`). This holds for
88	interpolation, loop and `set` bindings, `| string`, `| join`, sequence and map
89	literals, standout's own filters, and table cells:
90	
91	```jinja
92	{{ flag }}                {# true #}
93	{{ missing }}             {# none #}
94	{{ flags }}               {# [true, false, none] #}
95	{{ flags | join(", ") }}  {# true, false, none #}
96	```
97	
98	Two exceptions:
99	
100	- The `~` concatenation operator formats inside MiniJinja's evaluator, which
101	  exposes no hook: `{{ "x" ~ flag }}` yields `xTrue`. Write `{{ "x" }}{{ flag }}`
102	  or `{{ "x" ~ flag | string }}`.
103	- Structured output (JSON, YAML, XML, CSV) skips templates entirely and
104	  serializes your data directly, so those modes follow their format's own rules.
105	
106	If you build a `minijinja::Environment` yourself, use
107	`standout_render::template::new_environment()` — or call `register_filters` on
108	your own environment, which installs the same spelling.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## The Trailing-Newline Contract
113	
114	Two things happen to the newline at the end of a template, and together they
115	are observable in the bytes a script reads, so they are stated here rather than
116	discovered by probing.
117	
118	**The engine consumes exactly one final newline.** This is Jinja's rule and
119	MiniJinja keeps it. A template file ending in a single `\n` renders with no
120	trailing newline at all; a file ending in two renders with one.
121	
122	| Template source | Rendered string |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| `{{ name }}` | `x` |
125	| `{{ name }}\n` | `x` |
126	| `{{ name }}\n\n` | `x\n` |
127	| `{{ name }}\n\n\n` | `x\n\n` |
128	
129	**The process edge appends exactly one newline.** `App::run` writes a handled
130	command's text with `writeln!`, so what reaches stdout is the rendered string
131	plus one `\n` — whatever the template ended with.
132	
133	The practical consequence: a template that ends with one newline and a template
134	that ends with none produce identical bytes. To end a page with a blank line,
135	the template needs *two* trailing newlines. Every editor that adds a final
136	newline on save is therefore invisible here, which is the reason the rule is
137	worth stating.
138	
139	`standout-render/tests/trailing_newline.rs` pins the engine half;
140	`final_emission_routes_success_and_diagnostics_to_distinct_streams` in
141	`standout/src/cli/builder/execution.rs` pins the process half.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Style Tags
146	
147	Style tags use BBCode-like bracket notation to apply named styles from your theme:
148	
149	```jinja
150	[style-name]content to style[/style-name]
151	```
152	
153	### Basic Usage
154	
155	```jinja
156	[title]Report Summary[/title]
157	[error]Something went wrong![/error]
158	[muted]Last updated: {{ timestamp }}[/muted]
159	```
160	
161	### Nesting
162	
163	Tags can nest properly:
164	
165	```jinja
166	[outer][inner]nested content[/inner][/outer]
167	```
168	
169	### Spanning Lines
170	
171	Tags can span multiple lines:
172	
173	```jinja
174	[panel]
175	This is a multi-line
176	block of styled content
177	[/panel]
178	```
179	
180	### With Template Logic
181	
182	Style tags and MiniJinja work together seamlessly:
183	
184	```jinja
185	[title]{% if custom_title %}{{ custom_title }}{% else %}Default Title{% endif %}[/title]
186	
187	{% for task in tasks %}
188	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
189	{% endfor %}
190	```
191	
192	The second example shows dynamic style names—the style applied depends on the value of `task.status`.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Processing Modes
197	
198	Pass 2 (BBParser) processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
199	
200	| Mode | Behavior | Use Case |
201	| ------ | ---------- | ---------- |
202	| `Term` | Replace tags with ANSI escape codes | Rich terminal output |
203	| `Text` | Strip tags completely | Plain text, pipes, files |
204	| `TermDebug` | Keep tags as literal text | Debugging, testing |
205	
206	### Processing Modes Example
207	
208	Template: `[title]Hello[/title]`
209	
210	- **Term**: `\x1b[1;36mHello\x1b[0m` (rendered as cyan bold)
211	- **Text**: `Hello`
212	- **TermDebug**: `[title]Hello[/title]`
213	
214	### Setting the Mode
215	
216	```rust
217	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
218	
219	// Rich terminal
220	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
221	
222	// Plain text
223	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
224	
225	// Debug (tags visible)
226	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
227	
228	// Auto-detect based on TTY
229	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
230	```
231	
232	### Auto Mode
233	
234	`OutputMode::Auto` detects the appropriate mode:
235	
236	- If stdout is a TTY with color support → `Term`
237	- If stdout is a pipe or redirect → `Text`
238	
239	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` CLI flag automatically sets the output mode. See standout documentation for details.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Built-in Filters
244	
245	Beyond MiniJinja's standard filters, `standout-render` provides formatting filters:
246	
247	### Column Formatting
248	
249	```jinja
250	{{ value | col(10) }}                              {# pad/truncate to 10 chars #}
251	{{ value | col(20, align="right") }}               {# right-align in 20 chars #}
252	{{ value | col(15, truncate="middle") }}           {# truncate in middle #}
253	{{ value | col(15, truncate="start", ellipsis="...") }}
254	```
255	
256	### Padding
257	
258	```jinja
259	{{ "42" | pad_left(8) }}      {# "      42" #}
260	{{ "hi" | pad_right(8) }}     {# "hi      " #}
261	{{ "hi" | pad_center(8) }}    {# "   hi   " #}
262	```
263	
264	### Truncation
265	
266	```jinja
267	{{ long_text | truncate_at(20) }}                   {# "Very long text th..." #}
268	{{ path | truncate_at(30, "middle", "...") }}      {# "/home/.../file.txt" #}
269	{{ text | truncate_at(20, "start") }}              {# "...end of the text" #}
270	```
271	
272	### Display Width
273	
274	```jinja
275	{% if value | display_width > 20 %}
276	  {{ value | truncate_at(20) }}
277	{% else %}
278	  {{ value }}
279	{% endif %}
280	```
281	
282	Returns visual width (handles Unicode—CJK characters count as 2).
283	
284	### Style Application
285	
286	```jinja
287	{{ value | style_as("error") }}                    {# wraps in [error]...[/error] #}
288	{{ task.status | style_as(task.status) }}         {# dynamic: [pending]pending[/pending] #}
289	```
290	
291	---
292	
293	## Template Registry
294	
295	When using the `Renderer` struct, templates are resolved by name through a registry:
296	
297	```rust
298	use standout_render::Renderer;
299	
300	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
301	
302	// Add inline template
303	renderer.add_template("greeting", "Hello, [name]{{ name }}[/name]!")?;
304	
305	// Add directory of templates
306	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
307	
308	// Render by name
309	let output = renderer.render("greeting", &data)?;
310	```
311	
312	### Resolution Priority
313	
314	1. **Inline templates** (added via `add_template()`)
315	2. **Directory templates** (from `add_template_dir()`)
316	
317	### File Extensions
318	
319	Supported extensions (in priority order): `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`
320	
321	When you request `"report"`, the registry checks:
322	
323	- Inline template named `"report"`
324	- `report.jinja` in registered directories
325	- `report.jinja2`, `report.j2`, `report.stpl`, `report.txt` (lower priority)
326	
327	The `.stpl` extension is for SimpleEngine templates. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for details.
328	
329	### Template Names
330	
331	Template names are derived from relative paths:
332	
333	```text
334	templates/
335	├── greeting.jinja       → "greeting"
336	├── reports/
337	│   └── summary.jinja    → "reports/summary"
338	└── errors/
339	    └── 404.jinja        → "errors/404"
340	```
341	
342	---
343	
344	## Including Templates
345	
346	Templates can include other templates using MiniJinja's include syntax:
347	
348	```jinja
349	{# main.jinja #}
350	[title]{{ title }}[/title]
351	
352	{% include "partials/header.jinja" %}
353	
354	{% for item in items %}
355	  {% include "partials/item.jinja" %}
356	{% endfor %}
357	
358	{% include "partials/footer.jinja" %}
359	```
360	
361	This enables reusable components across your application.
362	
363	---
364	
365	## Context Variables
366	
367	Beyond your data, you can inject additional context into templates:
368	
369	```rust
370	use standout_render::{render_with_vars, OutputMode};
371	use std::collections::HashMap;
372	
373	let mut vars = HashMap::new();
374	vars.insert("version", "1.0.0");
375	vars.insert("app_name", "MyApp");
376	
377	let output = render_with_vars(
378	    "{{ app_name }} v{{ version }}: {{ message }}",
379	    &data,
380	    &theme,
381	    OutputMode::Term,
382	    vars,
383	)?;
384	```
385	
386	When handler data and context variables have the same key, **handler data wins**. Context is supplementary.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## Structured Output
391	
392	For machine-readable output (JSON, YAML, CSV), templates are bypassed entirely:
393	
394	```rust
395	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
396	
397	// Template is used for Term/Text modes
398	// Data is serialized directly for Json/Yaml/Csv
399	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
400	```
401	
402	| Mode | Behavior |
403	| ------ | ---------- |
404	| `Term` | Render template, apply styles |
405	| `Text` | Render template, strip styles |
406	| `TermDebug` | Render template, keep style tags |
407	| `Json` | `serde_json::to_string_pretty(data)` |
408	| `Yaml` | `serde_yaml::to_string(data)` |
409	| `Csv` | Flatten and format as CSV |
410	
411	This means your serializable data types automatically support structured output without additional code.
412	
413	---
414	
415	## Validation
416	
417	Check templates for unknown style tags before deploying:
418	
419	```rust
420	use standout_render::validate_template;
421	
422	let errors = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme);
423	if !errors.is_empty() {
424	    for error in &errors {
425	        eprintln!("Unknown style tag: [{}]", error.tag_name);
426	    }
427	}
428	```
429	
430	Validation catches:
431	
432	- Misspelled style names
433	- References to undefined styles
434	- Mismatched opening/closing tags
435	
436	---
437	
438	## API Reference
439	
440	### Render Functions
441	
442	```rust
443	use standout_render::{
444	    render,                  // Basic: template + data + theme
445	    render_with_output,      // With explicit output mode
446	    render_with_mode,        // With output mode + color mode
447	    render_with_vars,        // With extra context variables
448	    render_auto,             // Auto-dispatch template vs serialize
449	    render_auto_with_context,
450	};
451	
452	// Basic
453	let output = render(template, &data, &theme)?;
454	
455	// With output mode
456	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
457	
458	// With color mode override (for testing)
459	let output = render_with_mode(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term, ColorMode::Dark)?;
460	
461	// Auto (template for text modes, serialize for structured)
462	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
463	```

1	# Styled Help
2	
3	Standout can replace clap's built-in help with themed, template-driven output. Instead of clap's fixed format, your `--help` renders through the same MiniJinja + style-tag pipeline as the rest of your CLI.
4	
5	This gives you bold headers, consistent alignment, and a "Learn More" section linking to help topics. For CLIs with many commands, you can organize subcommands into named groups with section headers, help text, and visual separators.
6	
7	## Help Handling
8	
9	Help interception is **on by default**. An app that configures nothing renders
10	themed help; `.help_handling(false)` gives clap's own help back:
11	
12	```rust
13	// Themed help, no call needed.
14	App::builder().build()?;
15	
16	// Clap's own help instead.
17	App::builder().help_handling(false).build()?;
18	```
19	
20	With help handling on, standout:
21	
22	1. Disables clap's default `help` subcommand and registers its own (with `--page` for pager support), subject to the [install policy](#the-help-word) below
23	2. **Keeps** clap's native `--help`/`-h` flag, on purpose: clap's flag short-circuits argument validation, so `myapp build --help` renders even when required arguments are missing
24	3. Intercepts all help requests and renders them through a MiniJinja template with style tags — the `help` word, which clap routes like any other subcommand, and clap's `DisplayHelp` (from `--help`/`-h`, at root and subcommand level)
25	
26	Every form that is available renders the same help, through the same template and theme — with one exception, which is about the *form*, not the entry point: `--output` reaches the `help` word but not the flags. `myapp help --output text` renders in text mode; `myapp --help --output text` renders in the app's [output-mode fallback](./app-configuration.md#output-mode-fallback) (`Auto` unless the app sets one) and the typed mode is ignored. The reason is where each form is answered: the word is a subcommand, so clap parses its line in full, globals included, while `--help` short-circuits inside clap before the parse completes — so there are no matches to read a mode from when its `DisplayHelp` is rendered.
27	
28	Subcommand-level help (e.g. `myapp build --help`) also works, rendering that subcommand's help through standout.
29	
30	**Incompatible with the opt-out:** `command_groups` and topics need help interception to render. Configuring either alongside `.help_handling(false)` returns a `SetupError` from `build()`.
31	
32	### Whichever entry point you use
33	
34	Help is answered the same way through both parse paths — `run()` / `run_with()` and `get_matches_from()`. Same install policy for the word, same interception of `--help` / `-h`, same rendering: an application's entry point is not a fact about what `myapp help` means.
35	
36	The one thing the two paths cannot share is `--page`, because paging is a terminal side effect and only a *printing* entry point may perform it. `run()` hands the text to the pager; the capture APIs return it instead — `run_with()` marks it `SuccessKind::PagedHelp`, `get_matches_from()` returns `HelpResult::PagedHelp` — and leave the decision to you.
37	
38	## The `help` Word
39	
40	`--help` and `-h` are flags: they are always available and can never collide with your data. A bare `help` is different — at the root of a CLI with no subcommands, a bare word is *data*. `echo help`, `grep help`, and `ls help` all treat it as such, and a tool whose positional is a revision range or a file name would be wrong to swallow it.
41	
42	So standout only installs the word where it knows nothing else can claim it:
43	
44	| Root shape | `help` word |
45	| --- | --- |
46	| Has subcommands | Installed — a bare word there is already a command |
47	| Flat, no positionals | Installed — nothing to collide with |
48	| Flat, with positionals | **Opt-in only** — see below |
49	
50	For the third shape, only your application knows whether its positional domain excludes the word. Opt in with `.help_word(true)`:
51	
52	```rust
53	// `mytool <RANGE>` — a revision range is never the word "help".
54	App::builder().help_word(true).build()?;
55	```
56	
57	Opting in accepts the cost: the literal word `help` can no longer reach the positional, and `--` becomes the escape for it — `mytool -- help` passes the string through. Without the opt-in, `--help` / `-h` remain the only spelling, and they still render themed help.
58	
59	`help_word(true)` only ever *adds* the word; it is not a way to suppress `help` on a CLI that has subcommands. It cannot be combined with `.help_handling(false)` — the word is standout's own subcommand, so `build()` returns a `SetupError` without interception.
60	
61	### On a flat CLI, the word describes a flat CLI
62	
63	Clap's `help` is worded for a CLI with subcommands — "Print this message or the
64	help of the given subcommand(s)". On a flat CLI that sentence points at a
65	namespace that cannot exist, and the flat shape is exactly the one
66	`help_word(true)` serves. So the word describes the shape it is installed on:
67	
68	| Root shape | `help` about |
69	| --- | --- |
70	| Has subcommands | Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s) |
71	| Flat | Print this message |
72	
73	A flat CLI also drops the COMMANDS section entirely when `help` would be its
74	only entry. The word is machinery standout installs, not part of your surface,
75	and a section listing nothing but the command that printed it is noise:
76	
77	```text
78	COMMANDS
79	  help          Print this message
80	```
81	
82	Registered topics earn the section back, because `help <topic>` is then a real
83	destination and the word is how a reader reaches it. A root with commands of its
84	own always keeps its section, `help` included.
85	
86	### If your CLI already has a `help`
87	
88	Where standout installs the word, the name is standout's. An application that claims it too — a clap subcommand called `help` (or aliased to it), or a registration whose first path segment is `help` (`.command_with("help", …)`, `.command_with("help.topic", …)`, a `.commands(|g| g.group("help", …))`) — is a configuration standout refuses rather than serves:
89	
90	```text
91	duplicate command: help — this application's clap `Command` declares `help` (as a
92	subcommand name or alias), and standout installs a `help` word of its own, since
93	help handling is on by default. Rename the application's command, or call
94	.help_handling(false) to keep the name (help is then clap's own, and
95	command_groups and topics become unavailable)
96	```
97	
98	Each spelling is caught the moment it becomes visible: a registration under the root `help` fails `build()`, while a clap-declared one is only visible when your `Command` reaches a parse entry point, so it comes back as `HelpResult::Error` / `DispatchResult::Error` before anything is parsed. Neither reaches clap, whose answer to two subcommands of one name is a debug assertion — a panic on a configuration, which is what `SetupError` exists to prevent.
99	
100	Standing down — letting your `help` win and rendering nothing itself — is deliberately not offered. `myapp help` would then run your handler while `myapp --help` rendered standout's themed help: one CLI answering the same question two ways.
101	
102	Unaffected: a `help` deeper in the tree (`myapp db help` is yours, at a path the word is never installed on), and any root that never gets the word — a flat CLI with positionals and no `.help_word(true)`, or any CLI built with `.help_handling(false)`.
103	
104	### Why the word is reachable at all
105	
106	On a flat CLI whose root arguments are required, an injected `help` subcommand used to be advertised in help output and impossible to run: clap validates the root's requirements before routing, so `myapp help` failed with "the following required arguments were not provided" instead of printing help.
107	
108	The fix is a declaration, not a parser of standout's own. Where standout installs the word, it also sets clap's `subcommand_negates_reqs`, which suspends the root's requirements once a command is named — so `myapp help` routes to the word, while `myapp` on its own still reports its missing arguments and `myapp <RANGE>` still parses as data. The word's arguments (`myapp help topics`, `myapp help --page`, `myapp help --output text`) are clap's to parse, like any other subcommand's.
109	
110	The cost is worth naming: `subcommand_negates_reqs` applies to *your* subcommands too, so a root that declares required arguments stops requiring them once any command is named. That is why standout sets it only where it installs the word, and never on a CLI that did not get one. See [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).
111	
112	## Short and Long Help
113	
114	Clap gives a command a terse `about` and an optional full `long_about`, and its
115	convention is that `-h` shows the first while `--help` shows the second. Themed
116	help keeps that distinction:
117	
118	| Invocation | Renders |
119	| --- | --- |
120	| `-h` | `about` |
121	| `--help` | `long_about`, falling back to `about` |
122	| `help` | `long_about`, falling back to `about` — the spelled-out request reads like `--help` |
123	
124	Standout has to recover the spelling itself: `--help` short-circuits inside clap
125	and arrives as a `DisplayHelp` error that names neither the flag that raised it
126	nor the command it was raised for. Both are recovered from a *parse*, not from a
127	scan of the argument list — the two flags are re-declared as ordinary global
128	arguments on a throwaway clone whose own help flag is disabled, and clap
129	answers. That keeps `--` termination, `--flag=value`, short-option clusters, and
130	option-value consumption (`-o h` is not a help request) the parser's business,
131	per [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).
132	
133	Rendering help yourself with [`render_help`](#standalone-rendering) has no
134	invocation to classify, so it defaults to `HelpLength::Short`. Ask for the full
135	text with `length`:
136	
137	```rust
138	let config = HelpConfig {
139	    length: HelpLength::Long,
140	    ..Default::default()
141	};
142	```
143	
144	## What an Option Row Shows
145	
146	Option rows carry the information clap surfaces about an argument — its
147	value syntax, description, default, and accepted values:
148	
149	```text
150	OPTIONS
151	  --staged            Diff the staged changes
152	  --threshold <RATIO> Move/rename similarity threshold
153	  -c, --color <BOOL>  Enable ANSI color
154	  --output            Output format
155	                      default: auto
156	                      possible values: auto, term, text, term-debug, json, yaml, xml, csv
157	  --output-file-path  Write output to file instead of stdout
158	```
159	
160	The default and possible-value lines hang under the description column and
161	carry their own `[default]` and `[values]` tags, so a stylesheet can dim or
162	recolor them independently. Standout writes them as words rather than clap's
163	`[default: auto]` brackets: literal `[` would have to be escaped through the
164	style-tag parser, and the emphasis belongs to the theme. Hidden possible values
165	(`PossibleValue::hide`) are left out.
166	
167	Clap's own flags are rows like any other. The extractor reads the command
168	*after* clap builds it, which is when `-h`/`--help` and — for an application
169	that sets a version — `-V`/`--version` come into existence, so the page names
170	the flags it accepts instead of listing only what the application declared.
171	They sort last, after the application's own options.
172	
173	Options that take values render their metavar alongside the spelling, using an
174	explicit `value_name` when present and clap's fallback display otherwise. Pure
175	presence flags such as `ArgAction::SetTrue` and `SetFalse` do not render a
176	metavar and do not show parser-derived `true, false` values, because those words
177	are not valid command-line values for the flag.
178	
179	### Positionals get their own section
180	
181	Positionals render in an ARGUMENTS section ahead of OPTIONS, the way clap orders
182	them, rather than filed among the flags:
183	
184	```text
185	ARGUMENTS
186	  RANGE         Git range to diff, e.g. main..HEAD
187	
188	OPTIONS
189	  --staged      Diff the staged changes
190	```
191	
192	A positional is listed under its `value_name` when it declares one, else its
193	argument id, and is tagged `[metavar]`. The two sections size their columns
194	independently, so a long flag name does not push the ARGUMENTS column out with
195	it.
196	
197	## Styling User-Provided Strings
198	
199	When help interception is enabled, your clap `about` and `help` strings are rendered through standout's BBCode parser, so they can use any tag defined in your stylesheet:
200	
201	```rust
202	#[command(name = "myapp", about = "[bold]myapp[/bold] — a small CLI")]
203	struct Cli { /* ... */ }
204	```
205	
206	To emit a literal `[` or `]` in help text, escape it with a backslash: `\[` and `\]`. Other backslashes (file paths, regex examples like `\d+`) pass through unchanged. To emit a literal `\[`, write `\\[`.
207	
208	```rust
209	#[command(about = "Match pattern \\[regex: \\d+\\]")]
210	// renders as: Match pattern [regex: \d+]
211	```
212

236	## Command Groups
237	
238	CLIs with many commands (20+) benefit from organized help. The `CommandGroup` struct lets you split subcommands into named sections:
239	
240	```rust
241	use standout::cli::{App, CommandGroup};
242	
243	App::builder()
244	    .command_groups(vec![
245	        CommandGroup {
246	            title: "Commands".into(),
247	            help: None,
248	            commands: vec![
249	                Some("init".into()),
250	                Some("create".into()),
251	                Some("list".into()),
252	                Some("search".into()),
253	            ],
254	        },
255	        CommandGroup {
256	            title: "Per Pad(s)".into(),
257	            help: Some(
258	                "These commands accept one or more pad ids: <id> or ranges <id>-<id>\n\
259	                 ex: $ padz view 3 5 7-9  # views pads 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9".into()
260	            ),
261	            commands: vec![
262	                Some("open".into()), Some("view".into()), Some("peek".into()),
263	                None, // blank line separator
264	                Some("pin".into()), Some("unpin".into()),
265	                None,
266	                Some("complete".into()), Some("reopen".into()),
267	            ],
268	        },
269	        CommandGroup {
270	            title: "Misc".into(),
271	            help: None,
272	            commands: vec![
273	                Some("completions".into()),
274	                Some("help".into()),
275	                Some("config".into()),
276	            ],
277	        },
278	    ])
279	    .build()?;
280	```

311	### Blank Line Separators
312	
313	Use `None` entries in the `commands` vec to insert blank lines within a group. This creates visual sub-clusters without introducing nested group hierarchy:
314	
315	```rust
316	commands: vec![
317	    Some("open".into()),
318	    Some("view".into()),
319	    None,               // blank line
320	    Some("pin".into()),
321	    Some("unpin".into()),
322	],
323	```
324	
325	### Ungrouped Commands
326	
327	Commands that exist in your clap definition but don't appear in any `CommandGroup` are automatically appended to an "Other" section. This is a safety net: if you add a new subcommand but forget to add it to the group config, it still shows up in help. Silently hiding commands would be worse than slightly messy help.
328	
329	### Group Help Text
330	
331	Each group can include optional help text displayed between the section header and the command list. Use this to explain shared arguments, conventions, or usage patterns that apply to all commands in the group.
